    Current source review · 2026-09-28

    The Appropedia catalogue identifies Inmachines, a 600 × 400 mm work area and a 40 W CO₂ laser. Those specifications occur in both V1 and V2. The official V1 README describes LPC1768/grbl-LPC; the V2 README describes Teensy 4.1/grblHAL.

    The V2 sheet provides twelve printed terminal marks per X/Y driver, separate laser-PSU control and mains/tube-return marks, seven- and nine-terminal supply drawings, L/N/Earth power-entry nets, chiller lead marks 1 and 3 and tube electrode marks. The controller positions, splice entries, sensor/motor cable conductors and other unnumbered endpoints have explicit editorial identifiers. Extra blank driver squares and unidentified rectangles in the power-plug icon are not counted as proven contacts.

    The V2 BOM identifies DM556T drivers, LRS-100-24 and RSP-500-48A supplies, MYJG50W laser supply, LJ12A3-4-Z/AY probes, PS-3150 window sensor and CW-3000 chiller. These are design component identities, not fitted-hardware proof. The two DC supply drawings retain their seven-/nine-terminal descriptions without assigning an installed model or validating the drawn netlist.

    The HardwareX paper names Laser Controller PCB V1.7; the repository README links a shield path named V1-0. No connector schedule is imported across that unresolved revision boundary. The paper describes 24 V inductive probes, 3.3 V to 5 V laser signal conversion and an ATtiny startup gate delayed by 6 s. Original controller outputs must not be paralleled with SmoothieBox outputs, and the existing startup gate, window sensor and chiller circuit must not be bypassed.

    The chiller schematic labels only 1 and 3. The BOM reports a three-pole connector and three cores used while also specifying a two-core cable; the separate chiller cable is two-core. Its third pole is therefore listed with number and function unresolved, never as pin 2 or NC. Cable shields remain separate from cores and connector pins. USB and external-accessory pin schedules remain unknown.

    Potential STEP/DIR routes require an exact DM556T electrical contract, original-controller isolation, input topology, polarity, voltage, current, timing and return qualification. Sensor and laser candidates likewise lack the necessary interface and safe-startup evidence. This reference increment therefore selects zero function guesses and zero routes.

    Machine research dossier

    Creality Falcon2

    Evidence depth: diode laser model named in the wiki discovery section. This dossier is grounded in the Appropedia wiki entry only; references from that page to vendor, GitHub, or other non-wiki pages were not used as evidence.

    Wiki-supported identity and facts

    The Appropedia wiki names the Creality Falcon2 among diode-laser models. It does not give a power variant, bed size, control electronics, or pinout. Exact Falcon2 power variant is therefore unknown.

    Use, visuals, and electrical connections

    The captured wiki catalogue row does not provide a machine-specific operating procedure, connector table, electrical pinout, or transcribable wiring diagram for this model. Those items are recorded as unknown, rather than inferred from the model name or from the page's external links. The source may link further documentation, but that non-wiki content is outside this source-only research scope.

    Source

    • Tolocar / Open Source Machine Tools — Appropedia wiki — machine catalogue entry.

    Manufacturer-guide research · 2026-09-27

    The official Creality Falcon2 Quick Guide V2.0 describes a 22 W variant; this does not establish the wattage or revision installed on the Falcon2 named by the wiki. The guide’s printed p. 05 lists 100–240 V AC input, a 24.0 V DC / 5.0 A adapter output, 400 × 415 mm engraving area, and 455 ± 5 nm wavelength.

    The component overview (printed p. 06) names left/right Y-axis and front/rear X-axis assemblies, adapter board, 22 W laser module, control panel, emergency stop, security lock, TF slot, frame Type-C port, power input, and power button. The parts list (p. 07) names the power supply, air pump, USB-C cable, TF card/card reader, and USB-A-to-USB-C adapter. It also lists raiser stands, focus block, goggles, basswood, anti-static brush, storage box, hand tools, two lock keys, spare protective lens, screws, cleaning cloth, cable straps, metal protection plate, and tweezers. These supplied items are not assigned machine connector pins in the guide; the USB cables/adapters are accessories, not additional Falcon2 connector maps. The guide also describes AIR, FIRE, and LENS monitoring/indicators within the laser module (printed pp. 15–16); it publishes no separate external sensor contacts for them. The control-panel instructions name Frame, Start/Pause, and directional buttons, but give no panel electrical pinout. These are module/UI functions, not additional exposed machine pins. The guide does not provide machine-side motor, safety, panel, or harness cavity maps.

    Assembly instructions (pp. 09–10) describe a pump cable to the machine’s left-side pump interface and a laser-module cable to its adapter board. Neither cable has a published contact count, pin assignment, voltage, polarity, connector family, or mating-face view. The guide warns against connecting or disconnecting the laser-module cable while powered (p. 04). Both interfaces remain OPEN.

    The frame Type-C port supports host-computer operation with LaserGRBL/LightBurn (pp. 12–13); the module’s separate Type-C port is for firmware updates and work-log export (printed p. 16 / PDF p. 19). The guide gives neither port’s fitted-contact population, internal nets, or a SmoothieBox route. USB-IF’s 24-position receptacle map is eligible only as a generic form-only reference for each port. The TF slot remains position-unmapped: the SD Association distinguishes microSD assignments from its full-size SD schedule.

    USB Type-C receptacle form inventory · 24 positions per port

    USB-IF Specification R2.0, Table 3-4 supplies these standard receptacle position names. The two right-hand columns name the separate guide-identified ports; they do not assert fitted contacts or Falcon2 pin functions. All 48 port-position entries remain form-only and OPEN to SmoothieBox. This is a position-label inventory, not a mating-face drawing. A connector shell/shield is separate from the 24 contact designations; Falcon2 shell bonding is not documented and remains unmapped.

    Source dossier · Sculpfun SF-A9

    Evidence scope: the Appropedia catalogue identifies the SF-A9. Sculpfun's download center lists distinct 20 W and 40 W manuals. The inspected 20 W Version A manual is supplemental model-family evidence only; it does not identify the local unit's power variant, serial, controller, or wiring revision.

    Manual evidence

    The 140-page 20 W manual (PDF SHA-256 cc698ffa2c48b6b2ae29799fca84d955591b6c726250a54f0332f6b0878f91b0) was inspected at the machine overview and external-port diagrams, printed pp. 3–6. It names the data-line, air-pump, and power interfaces; identifies an emergency-stop knob, switch button, key switch, BT/Wi-Fi antenna, and laser head; and lists a rotary-axis motor wire accessory. The connection instructions describe USB/CH340 computer communication and the air-pump power cord. These labels establish peripheral roles only.

    No source contact count, numbered pin, connector standard (except the USB protocol context), polarity, voltage, current, motor-coil order, or laser-head signal assignment is provided for those groups. The 20 W laser head is included in that manual, but it must not be attributed to the unidentified local SF-A9.

    Complete wiki-researched machine dossier

    xTool S1 diode laser — Bristol Hackspace configuration

    Wiki evidence status: exact model-specific local operating and safety instructions. The wiki describes its installation and a 20 W laser module; this is not a claim that all S1 variants share the same module or configuration.

    Identity and configuration

    The local page identifies an xTool S1 diode laser using a 20 W, 455 nm blue diode. It lists a 608 × 385 mm bed, a maximum material thickness of 42 mm in the introductory description, and a 498 × 330 mm working area in the specification block. Those two areas differ; the wiki does not explain whether this reflects usable bed area versus motion/work area, so they are retained as separate source statements.

    The Bristol installation includes a honeycomb panel and air assist. With the honeycomb installed, the wiki gives a maximum material thickness of 15 mm. LightBurn is the local control workflow. The separate wiki setup guide specifies COM4, automatic air assist, the machine's homing and focus-probe sequence, and populating laser-offset values from the M1111 console output; it cautions that the Y offset may be better set to the datasheet's 21.8 value in some cases.

    Operation summary

    The local LightBurn guide calls for a visual work-area inspection, approved-material check, air-assist setting check, and confirmation that extraction starts with the isolator. The machine is homed before placing material. With the lid closed, the operator jogs the module, uses the focus probe's Detect operation, checks the origin and job origin in LightBurn, frames the job, then starts and continuously supervises the cut. The wiki says to remove waste and shut down the PC and isolator afterward.

    Materials and safety

    The wiki prohibits defeating the lid interlock or disabling fire detection, requires active supervision, and warns that the module can move with the lid open. PVC/vinyl, polycarbonate, ABS, PET/PETG, nylon, epoxy/resin, carbon-fibre composite, fibreglass, and other listed halogenated or flame-retardant materials are forbidden. Clear, white, or blue plastics are specifically excluded for this blue-light setup. The page identifies an emergency stop at the machine's rear right, an additional front pause button, software stop, and the isolator as stop methods.

    Diagram transcription and pinouts

    The local page includes annotated images for the rear-right emergency stop and front pause/controls, plus LightBurn screenshots for connection, homing, focus, offset, origin, framing, and layer settings. Textual location evidence is sufficient to record that the emergency stop is at the back-right side; the photographs were not recoverable through the search renderer in this pass. No electrical connector or laser-module pinout is published in the captured wiki pages.

    Sources

    • xTool S1 Diode Laser — local model identity, power/wavelength, areas, material restrictions, safety controls, and emergency-stop location.
    • xTool S1 — LightBurn — local software connection, focus, offset, origin, and job procedure.
    • Equipment catalogue — corroborates the xTool S1 listing.

    Unknowns: installed laser-module serial/revision, controller and firmware revisions, electrical pinouts, and the wiki's unexplained difference between nominal bed and working area dimensions.

    Wiki sources

    Sources are restricted to the supplied wiki-research dossier. External vendor/forum links are not used as evidence.

    Complete wiki-researched machine dossier

    Graphtec FC2200-90/EX

    Research status: wiki-sourced plotter/cutter dossier; exact model absent from the existing repository search. Captured 2026-09-23.

    Identity and documented workflow

    MakeICT lists the Graphtec FC2200-90/EX as an operational flatbed vinyl cutter/plotter. Its wiki guide documents an Inkscape-to-HPGL workflow:

    1. Create or import artwork in Inkscape, convert objects to paths, and inspect strokes with fills turned off.
    2. Save a copy as HPGL and set tool-offset correction to 0 for file export.
    3. Tape vinyl to the table, install the selected tool, and limit blade protrusion to the intended cut depth.
    4. Set condition values with the machine’s numbered panel buttons and run the built-in square/triangle test in unused media.
    5. Set lower-left and upper-right area points; upload the file through the machine’s local web interface and run the selected file.

    The wiki gives starting settings for a small blade (0.2 mm stickout, force 18, speed 10, quality 1), large blade (offset 28), and Sharpie (offset 0, force 5, speed 15, quality 1). These are MakeICT settings, not universal Graphtec parameters.

    Connections and pinout

    The wiki references a local upload interface but does not identify its physical network connector. No USB/serial/Ethernet, actuator, blade-force, sensor, power, or control-board pinout is present. The panel’s numbered setting controls are user-interface buttons, not pin numbers.

    Visual evidence

    The equipment inventory links to the machine page and its page describes test shapes; the inspected wiki text did not provide a wiring diagram. MakeICT Graphtec FC2200-90/EX wiki page.

    Limits

    The article says the machine “works” and the inventory lists it as operational. It does not establish firmware revision, serial number, supported media width, blade model, or electrical interface details. Do not convert cutter offset values into electrical assignments.

    Wiki sources

    Sources are restricted to the supplied wiki-research dossier. External vendor/forum links are not used as evidence.

    1. MakeICT Graphtec FC2200-90/EX wiki page

    Rev 8 uses a straight-through DB25 logic cable; DB25 pin 14 is 50 Hz VFD PWM and pin 16 charge-pump input requires >10 kHz. The 12-position terminal carries supply and field I/O; DB9 carries motor power. G540 Rev 8 manual; G540 setup guide.

    Documented evidence · unresolved wiring

    Documented / version scope: Manufacturer Rev 8 manual publishes all three separate domains: DB25 logic pins 2/3 X step/dir, 4/5 Y, 6/7 Z, 8/9 A; 10–13 inputs, 14 VFD PWM, 15 fault, 16 charge pump, 1/17 outputs, 18–25 GND. DB9 motor-power output pins 1/5 current-set resistor, 2–4 NC, 6 B, 7 /B, 8 A, 9 /A. 12-position main terminal 1–4 inputs, 5–6 outputs, 7 VFD GND, 8 VFD OUT, 9 VFD +10 V, 10 disable/E-stop, 11 +18–50 VDC, 12 supply GND. Manufacturer initial setup guide adds charge-pump >10 kHz and DB9 motor hookup. Rev 8 says DB25 cable must be straight-through. The DB9 is not a step/dir logic connector. A V2-Core could replace upstream controller logic while retaining G540 only under a separately verified electrical/interface design; do not connect V2 logic directly to motor-phase contacts.

    Documented / version scope: Manufacturer Rev 9.3 knowledge article explicitly lists DB25 output-capable pins 1–9, 14, 16, 17; dedicated inputs 10–13, 15; +5 V TTL signal domain; three relays; 0–10 V spindle analog converter. Caution: relay/analog outputs are C11G functions; a V2-Core retrofit would need its own compatible 0–10 V and isolation path, not a direct “same pin number” assumption.

    3DPrintMi

    Identity

    3DPrintMi is an open-frame RepRap printer design combining a Printrbot/Wallace-inspired layout with a fixed Y gantry. The wiki describes Mini, Plus and Aluminum Plus configurations; these are size/material variants under one design family and are counted as one machine identity here.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRap 3DPrintMi: design, feature set, build variants, specifications, videos and documentation links.
    • RepRap Wallace: source page for the related Wallace design.

    Specifications and operation

    The wiki lists the Mini at 152 × 152 × 152 mm and the Plus at 200 × 200 × 200 mm. It describes auto-levelling, a blower fan and extruder compatibility with Wade/Bowden or direct drive. Assembly is estimated at 2–3 hours excluding electronics; the wiki provides build manuals and assembly guides. The page reports 80–100 W for the stated hotend/bed conditions.

    Pinout and visuals

    No specific electronics revision or connector map is supplied in the captured article. The wiki includes assembly/printing videos and linked CAD; those should be checked for the exact build variant before transcribing any wiring.

    Wiki sources

    Sources are restricted to the supplied wiki-research dossier. External vendor/forum links are not used as evidence.

    3Drag FFF printer

    Identity

    The RepRap wiki identifies the Futura Elettronica/OpenElectronics 3Drag printer, release version 1.0. The structured specification calls its model “Mendel”; 3Drag is the named machine identity used here.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRap 3drag: specifications, photos, assembly sequence, wiring, limit-switch calibration and firmware variants.
    • RepRap 3Drag controller: A4988 stepper-driver and schematic/driver-image discussion.

    Specifications and operation

    The wiki lists a 200 × 200 × 200 mm envelope, four NEMA 17 steppers, 15 V/3 A maximum supply, FTDI USB-to-serial connection, 3 mm filament and nominal 120 mm/s speed. Its assembly chapters include Z limit installation, X/Y limit calibration and extruder-arm height adjustment. The page lists different display/controller variants, including no display, VM8201 and a RepRapDiscount full-graphic controller.

    Pinout and diagrams

    The controller article identifies A4988 drivers and describes STEP pulses and MS1/MS2/MS3 microstep selection. The surfaced source does not expose complete connector contact numbers or a full board pin map, so those remain unknown. Wiki images are labelled as schematic/driver images; confirm the specific VM8201/other controller revision before interpreting them.

    Limits

    The wiki's dimensional accuracy table contains an apparent Z-value anomaly; this dossier does not repeat it as a trusted performance figure.

    3Drag FFF printer

    Identity

    The RepRap wiki identifies the Futura Elettronica/OpenElectronics 3Drag printer, release version 1.0. The structured specification calls its model “Mendel”; 3Drag is the named machine identity used here.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRap 3drag: specifications, photos, assembly sequence, wiring, limit-switch calibration and firmware variants.
    • RepRap 3Drag controller: A4988 stepper-driver and schematic/driver-image discussion.

    Specifications and operation

    The wiki lists a 200 × 200 × 200 mm envelope, four NEMA 17 steppers, 15 V/3 A maximum supply, FTDI USB-to-serial connection, 3 mm filament and nominal 120 mm/s speed. Its assembly chapters include Z limit installation, X/Y limit calibration and extruder-arm height adjustment. The page lists different display/controller variants, including no display, VM8201 and a RepRapDiscount full-graphic controller.

    Pinout and diagrams

    The RepRap assembly page's original connector/wiring diagram is a machine-side source image, not a controller pinout. Its rendered labels establish connector groups and functional paths, but it gives no numbered contacts or connector-face view.

    Diagram label / groupSource-supported relationshipContact-level detail not established
    X motor, Y motor, Z motor, E motorFour separate motor cable groups connect to matching X, Y, Z and E motor outputs on the 3Drag controller. The assembly procedure describes 4-conductor, 0.5 mm² motor cable.Coil/contact order, cavity numbering, phase polarity and connector view. Do not infer a motor pin order from the schematic's drawn wire colours.
    X home, Y home, Z homeThree separate home microswitch cable groups are shown at the controller. Assembly text names each cable and says they connect to the board's pin strips.Pin numbers, switch contact selection, active polarity and connector view.
    Heated bedA separate two-conductor path is drawn between the bed and board output.Polarity, connector contact order and current rating.
    Extruder heater and thermistorThe schematic shows separate extruder-heater and thermistor connections. The controller article documents two temperature-sensor inputs and MOSFET outputs for extruder and bed heaters.Header contact numbers, thermistor curve, heater voltage/current and installed board revision.
    Thermistor, fanThe schematic labels the thermistor and fan groups; the controller description documents a low-tension fan output.Contact positions, fan voltage/current and sensor wiring order.
    Power supplyA two-wire supply path feeds the board. The assembly page explicitly says to set the power supply to 15 V.Board terminal polarity/contact view and exact supply/board revision.
    PC USBA USB cable connects the PC to the board's Mini-USB connector. The controller source identifies an FT232RL USB/serial interface used for programming and PC control.USB connector contacts and any electrical protection details.

    The controller article identifies its own release version 1.0 as an ATmega2560 board based on Sanguinololu, with up to four Pololu-compatible stepper drivers and A4988 driver circuitry described in its schematic section. That board architecture is not proof that every 3Drag machine uses this exact electronics revision: the printer page lists multiple display/controller options, including no display, VM8201 and a RepRapDiscount full-graphic controller. Keep those variants separate. No complete numbered machine-side or board-header contact map was recovered.

    Limits

    The wiki's dimensional accuracy table contains an apparent Z-value anomaly; this dossier does not repeat it as a trusted performance figure.

    The original wiring diagram's source page and image identify the depicted functional groups only; there is no labelled mating/board view. The source images were inspected directly from the linked wiki asset, but the exact physical installation and board revision of an individual 3Drag remain unverified. Do not draw or use this material as a reconnectable pin-by-pin map.

    Contact representation and route decision

    The inventory contains 56 individually represented reference entries on 18 cards: 16 motor-output contacts, 9 board HOME contacts, 9 separately drawn switch lugs, 8 heater contacts, 4 thermistor circles, 2 FAN contacts, 2 PWR contacts, 2 alternative PL1 symbols and 4 explicitly drawn USB positions. These are not 56 verified physical contacts on the fitted printer. Three switch middle lugs have source_unlisted roles. Cable-core counts create no extra connector contacts or numbered cores.

    Motor 1B/1A/2A/2B contacts are post-driver winding outputs. They must not be equated with SmoothieBox STEP/DIR/ENABLE inputs. Board HOME S and ground are source-circuit roles; no individual C/NC lug-to-header relationship or SmoothieBox MIN/MAX choice is selected. JPV-selected supply is recorded as a source reference, without asserting the installed voltage. NC means normally closed at the switch; atlas OPEN means no selected route.

    Repeated heater marks remain +, +, -, -. The identifiers upper +, lower +, upper -, lower - are unique p.4 schematic locators, not silkscreen numbers or physical cavities. THERM1/THERM2 upper circle and lower circle are p.5 schematic locators for unnumbered symbols. Header mark listing order is not the physical mating view.

    HEATER1 is the extruder output and HEATER2 the heated-bed output. Four header contacts remain listed even when the load cable has two conductors. FAN+ is connected to +Vin in the schematic; the separate 12 V / 100 mA accessory description does not prove a regulated 12 V rail. PWR is a connector name; its source marks are + and -. PL1 is an alternative supply input; no simultaneous PWR/PL1 feed is selected or additional jack-switch contacts inferred. USB position 4 is omitted by this schematic, not declared NC; no full physical Mini-USB cavity inventory is claimed.

    Choose no guess for any of the 56 entries. The source supplies no jointly qualified reference endpoint, installed harness and complete SmoothieBox electrical endpoint. The violet dotted GUESS legend stays visible; there are zero route instances. No DB25 is evidenced in this scoped inventory. ICSP, configuration/programming jumpers, expansion contacts and driver-module sockets are outside this audit of the existing 14 groups; it is not a complete controller netlist.

    Source boundaries and remaining qualification

    The manual distinguishes 3DCONTR-DRIVER from 3DCONTROLLER without driver modules and says the bed option is not factory-enabled in either. Do not transfer this inventory to an unidentified Sanguinololu, VM8201, display or other board variant. The earlier wiki 15 V / 3 A specification and the manufacturer controller recommendations of 15 V / 5 A without a bed and at least 10 A with a bed are separate source scopes. Neither establishes the installed supply.

    The Futura product page identifies SKU 7350-3DCONTR-DRIVER under Descrizione. Its + e PWR wording is retained as a source discrepancy, not used as a third contact or negative-contact mark; manual pp.2–4 establish PWR/+ and PWR/-. The manual says supplied drivers are calibrated, while the product page says calibration is needed before use. Neither statement proves the fitted adjustment. The manufacturer circuit article under The diagram independently distinguishes motor winding outputs from STEP inputs and identifies HEATER1/extruder, HEATER2/bed, THERM1/extruder sensor and THERM2/bed sensor. The RepRap assembly and controller page provide machine/variant context; cable counts are not numbered-cavity evidence.

    Before any physical wiring, identify the fitted controller and options, obtain actual connector and cable views, measure continuity, identify motor windings and the replacement-driver interface, qualify heater/fan loads and protection, confirm complete thermistor curves and input conditions, select one power arrangement, and obtain the complete SmoothieBox electrical contract. Contact facts remain source references until those requirements are met.

    Adapto RepRap printer

    Identity

    Adapto is a configurable RepRap printer design. Its base-design BOM identifies five mechanical motor locations (X, Y, two Z, and extruder E), while its electronics note requests four stepper channels and two heaters.     • RepRap Adapto: component lengths, frame assembly, mechanical construction and revision caveats.
    • Adapto Flex: a separate experimental toolhead-focused variant, linked here only for distinction.

    Construction and operation

    The guide gives an example using 20 × 20 mm extrusion, with 300 mm X, 340 mm Y and 420 mm Z frame members; it notes approximate lost travel from frame to usable travel. Its BOM identifies X, Y, two Z, and extruder E motor locations and lists a hot end plus heated bed. It cautions that parts may differ and upgrades may be missing.

    Pinout and visuals

    The base Adapto build guide gives a four-stepper/two-heater controller requirement but does not identify the installed board, wiring, or connector pinout. Its BOM lists one STL containing three endstop-holder parts; the upstream repository README separately lists the X-axis holder as a todo, so availability varies by revision. Neither source proves fitted switches. The linked Adapto Flex is a separate variant; its SmoothieBoard suggestion is not evidence for this base profile.

    Limits

    The cited build information is user-contributed and under construction. Confirm the selected frame dimensions, design revision, controller, harness, and fitted switch/heater configuration before wiring.

    Anycubic Kobra

    Identity and scope

    The Artisans Asylum machine page records Make “anyCubic”, Model “Kobra”, and Serial “Unknown”, and links a user manual. The exact model name is therefore supported; the physical unit’s serial, installed controller/board, and build revision remain unknown. This record does not cover Kobra 2, Neo, Go, Plus, Max, or another variant.

    Manual and source-labeled cable groups

    Anycubic’s 2022-11-24 manual, version 0.0.5, shows four cable groups: 1 Print head, 2 X-axis motor, 3 Touchscreen, and 4 Z-axis motor. Those numerals label groups in the illustration, not contact or cavity positions. The manual gives no connector pin counts, mating-face orientation, pin functions, conductor order, polarity, or machine-to-controller pin schedule. Its overview names a Y motor, but the four-group cable illustration does not identify a Y-motor cable; no Y harness is inferred.

    The manual says to match cable labels to ports and not connect or disconnect cables while powered. Its model specifications list 110/220 V AC, 50/60 Hz, 400 W, a 260 °C maximum extruder temperature, and a 110 °C maximum bed temperature; these are not connector ratings or retrofit assignments.

    Other documented features and unresolved geometry

    The product overview also labels a proximity switch, data-cable port, memory-card slot, power switch, and voltage selector. The manual says the proximity switch detects the metal bed for automatic leveling. These are contextual features only; the cited sources provide no contact schedule for them. The Artisans page gives a 200 × 200 mm stage, while the manufacturer manual gives a 220 × 220 × 250 mm build size. These are distinct source claims and are left unresolved.

    The examined sources do not establish a DB25 connector on this physical unit. This is not a claim that the unit has none. No DB25 peripheral, controller connector, or SmoothieBox route is inferred.

    3DMakerWorld Artifex

    Identity

    Artifex is a 3DMakerWorld open-source desktop FFF printer design based partly on MendelMax 1.5/2.0. It remains a distinct design with its own frame, electrical and mechanical specification.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRap Artifex, revision 114817: model description, design-reported electrical/mechanical specifications, and links to named documents.
    • Artifex User Manual (January 2014 mirror): named manufacturer document; third-party hosted copy. Artifex design repository: published mechanical files and README; no electrical schematic or harness schedule. Current 3DMakerWorld Support: Artifex 2 material kept separate from this legacy profile.

    Specifications and operation

    The versioned Artifex design record names RAMBo electronics, a MakerGear hot end with a 0.35 mm nozzle, a 24 V / 200 W heated bed, three 24 V cooling fans (filament drive, print surface, electronics), 110/220 VAC power requirements, X/Y linear-rail and GT2-belt motion, and Z precision shafts with ACME leadscrews. These are design facts, not external connector assignments or a fitted-unit inspection.

    Pinout and visuals

    No per-contact harness map was found in the accessible, captured excerpts and inspected sources. RAMBo board terminal and firmware labels do not identify the Artifex external harness. No DB25 is evidenced, and the 110/220 VAC requirement is context only, not a SmoothieBox route. The named hot end, bed, fans, and motion references are not mapped to SmoothieBox contacts.

    Limits

    The specifications apply to the Artifex wiki design record. Verify the actual RAMBo revision, hotend and bed before wiring.

    Wiki sources

    Source scope and limits are documented in the research dossier. Artifex 2 material is not substituted for the legacy design.

    Bambu Lab P1S

    Evidence scope: The exact-model Bambu Lab Quick Start Guide and two Bambu replacement-part listings support the facts below. These sources do not identify the fitted unit's board or cable revision, provide a mating-face view, or establish a SmoothieBox connection. The Appropedia catalogue entry supports model identity only.

    Official P1S guide

    The 2023 Quick Start Guide (document Y.BC.SM.A00201-01) labels the rear USB port, a four-pin Bambu Bus port and the mains power socket. Its component drawing also identifies the screen/LCD cable and Micro SD slot. The guide names a Dual-Core Cortex M4 motion controller and five closed-loop fan functions: Part Cooling, Hot End, Control Board, Chamber Temperature Regulator and Auxiliary Part Cooling. It does not provide contact functions or mating-face orientation for these interfaces.

    The guide rates the rear USB output at 5 V / 1.5 A and the input at 100–240 VAC, 50/60 Hz, with maximum power of 1000 W at 220 V or 350 W at 110 V. These are source specifications, not a SmoothieBox wiring plan. The mains socket is context only. Fan names are functional context; connector counts, per-contact roles and harness mapping are not given.

    OPEN contact inventory

    The current source overlay lists 34 OPEN positions: 6 and 12 on the two ends of the P1 Series toolhead cable; 6 and 6 on the ends of the heatbed signal cable; and 4 at the rear Bambu Bus port. Each displayed number is an editorial inventory index, not a source-stamped cavity number. The listings do not assign individual signals or identify installed cable revision and end orientation. All positions remain OPEN, with zero proposed routes and zero guesses.

    The USB port, mains socket, screen/LCD cable and Micro SD slot remain named peripherals without contact schedules in the cited evidence. This profile does not establish stepper-driver terminals, endstop wiring or an external DB25 connector. Do not transfer generic controller or printer pinouts to the P1S.

    Official P1P guide

    The 2023 English Quick Start Guide (16 pages, document issue as cited by Bambu) labels the Tool Head, SD Card, Screen, rear USB Charging Port, four-pin Bambu Bus port and Power Socket. It identifies a 2.7-inch display, Micro SD storage, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/Bambu Bus connectivity and a Dual-Core Cortex M4 motion controller. This component/location guide is not a pin schedule.

Neither listing assigns individual contacts or confirms the fitted revision.

    Cartesio V0.5 3D printer

    Identity

    The RepRap wiki identifies Cartesio V0.5 as a professional-grade FFF printer design. Its general page also shows related W0.9, M0.6 and LDMP configurations; this dossier covers the V0.5 identity only and does not count those as separate machines.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRap Cartesio: model generation, intended tooling, features and images.
    • RepRap machine list: design index.

    Operating information

    The page describes a rigid design intended to accept multiple tools and says machines include fume extraction and filtration. It lists dual contactless filament runout sensing and an anti-heater-ooze feature. A source recheck on 2026-09-28 found the linked RepRap Cartesio Build Manual is a red link rather than an existing manual page, while its external build-instructions link returns 404. No additional V0.5 wiring source was recovered through those links, and these feature descriptions do not identify electrical connector positions.

    Source-scoped machine interfaces

    The model page names the fume-extraction/filtration unit, dual contactless filament-runout sensing, and anti-heater-ooze feature. These are functional descriptions only: no connector designators, terminal numbers, mating views, electrical levels, polarity, or harness mapping are supplied. “Can hold multiple tools” is a mechanical capability, not proof of a fitted toolchanger or its signals. Keep each feature as an OPEN context group until a V0.5-specific schematic, manual page, or clear connector photograph establishes its actual contacts.

    Pinout and visuals

    The wiki page includes images of several Cartesio variants and extruders. Its V0.5 description does not identify the installed controller, stepper-driver board, motor or endstop connectors, heater/thermistor contacts, fan outputs, sensor terminal positions, or external I/O. No version-specific connector pinout was found; do not infer contacts from mechanical photographs or transfer assignments from W0.9, M0.6, or LDMP.

    Limits

    The wiki's claimed toolchanger and material-extrusion features appear in a “things to come” list and are not treated as installed features. Verify the exact Cartesio generation before relying on operational details. This is model-level design evidence, not proof that an individual machine retains the listed features.

    Creality CR-10S

    Research updated 2026-09-27. MakeICT lists this model as retired. The installed unit’s board revision, firmware, maintenance, and modifications are unknown.

    Identity and configuration

    The MakeICT wiki reports a 300 × 300 × 400 mm build volume, PLA/ABS use, 1.75 mm filament, 0.4 mm nozzle, nozzle maximum 250 °C, and bed maximum 100 °C. These are wiki entries, not measurements of the retired unit. The page’s stock image does not establish the physical unit’s condition.

    Manufacturer manual and harness contacts

    The Creality-branded CR-10 Series User Manual V5.1 explicitly names CR-10S in its model scope; the available copy is hosted by a third-party mirror rather than an official Creality domain. Page 4 (PDF page 9) shows four six-position/four-wire stepper groups (X/Y/Z/E) and three three-position/two-wire limit-switch groups (X/Y/Z), matched by yellow labels. The motor and switch plugs appear as white rectangular housings. A separate photograph labels circular control-box ports as aviation connectors; it does not identify the motor or switch plug series. The diagram lists 24 plus 9 nominal form slots. Its stable 1–6 and 1–3 indices are editorial only, not cavity numbers or orientation: the manual supplies no conductor/cavity mapping, winding-pair assignment, limit polarity, or NO/NC state.

    Firmware/controller maps

    The Klipper 2017 CR-10S configuration and Creality factory firmware repository assign MCU or board logical pins to motion, endstop, heater, sensor, fan, and display functions. These firmware references do not identify external harness cavities or the MakeICT unit’s fitted board. They are not external peripheral pinouts and are not wired to SmoothieBox in this diagram. Klipper’s example bed section sets `max_temp: 130`, while the manual lists a 100 °C bed maximum; this software threshold does not establish a higher machine rating.

    Route status

    All 33 nominal manual-counted form slots remain OPEN; the manual does not assign individual cavity functions or conductor identities, and no SmoothieBox route is established. SmoothieBox MOTOR CONTROL contacts are STEP/DIR/ENABLE logic. Do not treat them as motor winding outputs or connect them directly to the CR-10S stepper leads. No documented external driver stage or MakeICT retrofit was found. Heater, bed, thermistor, fan, LCD, filament-sensor, USB/SD, and mains are editorial unresolved function buckets, not eight manufacturer-documented connectors. No revision-matched physical contact map was found for them.

    Sources and limits

    MakeICT CR-10S wiki page · MakeICT equipment inventory · Creality CR-10 Series User Manual V5.1 · Klipper 2017 CR-10S MCU map · Creality CR-10S firmware repository.

    Primary-source extension · BQ printer and recycler controller references

    The Appropedia-only findings above are preserved as the original source boundary. CubeFactory2's project repository identifies its printer as BQ Prusa i3 / Hephestos and names a Maxon ESCON 70/10 controller for the recycler brushless motor. BQ's Hephestos and ZUM repositories provide the 2015 revision-1.2 ZUM Mega 3D design-family schematic. This does not prove the exact installed board revision.

    The BQ drawing labels J8 thermistor pins 1–4 and J10 endstop pins 1–18, as well as J11 sensor and J12–J18 fan/heater boundaries. The Hephestos 2 DNP notes for J10, J11 and J13 are retained; J16 and J18 are marked DNP in the source. J9 is a crossed 3×4 alternate header with illegible contact numbering, so its 12 entries are explicitly editorial DNP inventory slots, not a numbered connector map.

    The Maxon ESCON 70/10 Hardware Reference supplies the separate J1–J7 controller connector family, including J5 digital I/O and J6 analog I/O. Its PWM set-value input allows a narrow, clearly marked guess from the proposed SmoothieBox PWM TOOL output; voltage, PWM settings, configuration, reference and safety prerequisites are stated beside the figure. The CubeFactory powertrain prose calls its 24 V temperature controller “Inkbird D1S-2R-24,” but the linked front-panel photograph shows INKBIRD / ITC without a full model. A manufacturer-branded SESTOS D1S-family manual copy conflicts with assigning that family’s terminals to the photographed controller, so the electrical boundary is shown OPEN with zero invented positions. The 24 V, 150 W sleeve draws 6.25 A nominally; the D1S-2R family manual's 3 A resistive rating at 250 V AC does not qualify the unidentified controller for that DC load. The actual model and any external rated switching stage remain unverified, so no heater route is shown.

    Sources and per-pin provenance: CubeFactory 2 evidence dossier. The older wiki-only statements above remain intact.

    Complete wiki-researched machine dossier

    Eventorbot RepRap printer

    Identity

    Eventorbot is an open-source printer design with a single steel frame. The RepRap wiki describes its goal as a rigid, low-cost machine with many printable parts.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRap Eventorbot: dimensions, parts list, drawings, upgrades, videos and assembly sequence.
    • RepRap machine index: model catalog.

    Specifications and operation

    The wiki lists a 152 × 152 × 152 mm print volume, 37 printed parts and 1.5 mm sheet steel frame stock. It links engineering drawings and sequential tutorials covering frame, X, Z, extruder and Y assembly. The wiki also describes a dual-extrusion upgrade. These are design-level notes, not verification of a physical machine.

    Electrical parts in the Eventorbot design BOM

    The RepRap Eventorbot 1.2 parts list names three four-wire NEMA 17 motors, a geared PG35L-048 extruder stepper, four push-button momentary endstop switches, a panel-mount 5.5 × 2.1 mm DC jack, and a 12 V / 5 A supply (12 A if the optional heated bed is used). Its hotend list includes a 5.6 Ω / 5 W resistor. It also lists a Sanguinololu 1.3a motherboard with stepper drivers. These are source design facts, not proof of a particular machine's installed parts.

    Sanguinololu 1.3a reference contacts

    The RepRap Sanguinololu page describes X/Y/Z/extruder driver sockets and three-position endstop headers. The outside endstop positions are GND and SIG (the page's prose does not say which is left or right); the center position supplies selectable 5 V or source voltage through the Stop Volt solder link. Its revision history says 1.3b2 changed the three-position endstop connector to a four-position CD-ROM form, which is not substituted here. Four 16-position driver-carrier socket schedules are retained as board-reference positions with functions unassigned. None establishes that a Sanguinololu board is fitted locally.

    Contact and route limits

    The source-counted four-wire motor leads are editorial conductor slots, not connector cavities. The extruder motor's lead map, endstop switch terminals, jack contact count/polarity, exact power option and complete harness census are not published. Every candidate remains OPEN; no SmoothieBox route or dotted guess is justified by these sources.

    Limits

    The performance claims about vibration are design rationale, not comparative test evidence. No local machine serial, controller, motor, harness, or wiring installation has been verified.

    Design and controller references

    These RepRap design pages support the listed design-BOM parts and the separate Sanguinololu 1.3a board reference. They do not establish a physical machine installation.

    FoldaRap 4.0

    Identity

    FoldaRap 4.0 is a foldable, portable RepRap printer design. The maker repository distinguishes its winter 2017 release from the separate FoldaRap 3.5 release. The cited design options do not prove a particular machine's fitted electronics.

    Generation-specific electronics evidence

    The maker's Item F 4.0 bill-of-materials column identifies five stepper motors (X, Y, two Z positions, and extruder), X/Y sensor microswitches with separate two-pin sensor leads, one two-pin fan lead, an E3D Lite6 hotend, two small fans, and a 90 W bed film with a 100 kΩ probe. The wiki describes external 12 V/24 V and internal PSU options. The Item F 4.0 BOM assigns quantity one to external 12 V 138 W; external 24 V 160 W entries have no quantity. The repository also contains Minitronics, Melzi, and Duet 2 WiFi configurations; none establishes the fitted controller or machine contact map.

    Contact and route limits

    • The X/Y sensor leads each have two individually listed, unnumbered harness positions. A dotted path to the corresponding SmoothieBox MIN SIGNAL/GND pair is a functional guess only. Switch-terminal choice, conductor order, polarity/logic, board fitment, and electrical compatibility remain unverified. SENSOR + is left open.
    • Motor contact positions and coil pairs, fan contacts, heater/thermistor positions, bed contacts, and PSU connector positions are not mapped by these sources. Their SmoothieBox routes remain OPEN.
    • The maker BOM lists a rear-plate Kycon KPJX-PM-4S jack and separately an unquantified shielded KPJX-PM-4S-S option. The exterior diagram lists manufacturer contacts 1, 2, 3, and 4 as individual reference positions, all FoldaRap functions and routes OPEN; only the shielded option adds shield tabs A and B, also individually shown and OPEN. No jack polarity or role is assigned.
    • The Item F 4.0 BOM also lists one EU power cord, one LCD specifically for Minitronics, and one USB cable. Their connector types and contact schedules are not documented; the diagram names each peripheral without inventing pin counts or routes.
    • SmoothieBox MOTOR CONTROL STEP/DIR/ENABLE pins are logic outputs for an external driver; do not connect motor windings directly. BED SWITCH CONTROL is not a bed-heater output: its cited Q3 stage is rated 60 V / 0.3 A, far below a direct 90 W heater load.
    • No inspected FoldaRap 4.0 source identifies a DB25 connector.

    Sources checked 2026-09-27

    • RepRap FoldaRap: generation-specific 4.0 design options and separate earlier-generation notes.
    • EmmanuelG/Foldarap maker repository: README release history, bill-of-materials workbook, firmware options, and hardware resources.
    • /home/arthur/dev/smoothie-box/docs/smoothie-central.html, Chapter 18: SmoothieBox exterior contact names and load-stage limit context.

    These are design-level facts and proposed function guesses, not an installed-machine pinout or authorization to connect unverified circuits. Check the exact machine revision and every contact before wiring.

    Formlabs Form 2 SLA printer

    Identity and operation

    RaumZeitLabor's wiki identifies the installed fab-lab printer as a Formlabs Form 2 and gives its network-print workflow. That local wiki is identity and operating-context evidence, not a hardware pinout.

    Formlabs hardware and external interfaces
    • The Form 2 product glossary identifies a 100–240 V internal power supply that converts line power to +24 V DC; three motherboard motor-driver chips drive the build-platform, wiper and tank-carrier steppers; a motherboard-to-front-display ribbon; built-in Wi-Fi; and rear-accessible USB and Ethernet ports.
    • Formlabs' connection instructions identify the Form 2 rear Ethernet connector as RJ-45 and list 10BASE-T/100BASE-TX. The diagram enumerates eight connector-reference positions without assigning Form 2 pin functions.
    • The same article describes the supplied USB cable as the wired computer connection but does not identify the Form 2 port subtype or contact schedule. Its USB-C statement applies to Form 4/Form 4L and is not transferred to Form 2.
    • Form 2 technical specifications list 100–240 V AC, 1.5 A, 50/60 Hz and 65 W. Connector type, terminal count and protective-earth mapping are not established by these reviewed sources.
    • Formlabs describes a 405 nm, 250 mW maximum violet diode laser with Class 1 classification. No external laser power supply or electrical contacts are documented for this printer.
    Pinout and route limits

    All eight RJ-45 positions, where individually shown, remain OPEN to SmoothieBox. USB, mains, motor, display-ribbon, Wi-Fi and laser contact schedules are unknown or internal. No external step/direction/enable input is documented for the Formlabs motherboard drivers. No SmoothieBox wire, guessed route or DB25 connector is established.

    Other limits

    Resin handling and post-processing instructions in the local wiki are incomplete. This wiring diagram does not serve as a service manual or authorize opening the printer or modifying mains, laser or internal motor circuits.

    RepRap Huxley (community design)

    Variant boundary

    This entry describes the general RepRap Huxley community design. The Huxley page links separate RepRapPro, TechZone and eMaker kit instructions; those kit implementations are not evidence for this profile. RIS 1 compliance permits alternative electronics and does not identify which controller, if any, is fitted to a particular Huxley.

    Source-supported peripherals and contacts
    • The Huxley design lists three NEMA 14 steppers and one NEMA 17 extruder stepper; the extruder is Bowden. It does not map the three smaller motors to axes or specify motor terminals, connectors, winding pairs, or cable order.
    • RIS 1 is a controller feature set: at least four stepper motors, three RIS 2 endstops, one thermistor sensor, and one heater of at least 60 W. It explicitly allows single-board or distributed electronics and does not prescribe system voltages.
    • RIS 2 defines a conditional 3-pin endstop header reference at 2.54 mm pitch, Molex KK100-compatible, with the standard diagram order Vs | GND | Vcc. It assigns no numeric pin numbers. The standard documents separate 3.3 V and 5 V electrical variants, and specifically says Sanguinololu 1.3a does not match this pinout; neither option is selected for this Huxley profile. These labels are standards references only; Huxley-specific fit, orientation, axis mapping and continuity are not established.
    • No machine-side DB25, fitted SmoothieBox connector map, endstop harness or machine-specific electrical pinout was identified. All SmoothieBox routes remain OPEN and no guess is drawn.

    LulzBot Mini

    Research status: wiki-sourced model dossier covering two SoMakeIt installations of the same model; exact model absent from the frozen atlas and exact-name repository search. Captured 2026-09-23.

    Wiki-recorded installations

    The SoMakeIt wiki describes Mini 1 and Mini 2 as LulzBot Mini units with a 152 × 152 × 158 mm print volume and 0.5 mm nozzle. Mini 1 has a PEI bed and is listed for PLA, ABS and PETG. Mini 2 has a glass bed and a “Flexystruder”; its listed purpose is flexible filament such as TPU and NinjaFlex. The two units share an OctoPrint address according to the page; the page says to ensure the service is attached/shared with the intended unit.

    The same page lists Mini 1 as stored and not in active use after the resin printer arrived; Mini 2’s status is “under investigation.” Keep these instance statuses separate.

    Workflow and use

    The wiki names Cura for slicing, with printing either directly from Cura or through OctoPrint. It says material and bed configuration differ between the two instances; do not reuse Mini 1’s material list as confirmation for Mini 2.

    Connections and pinout

    The wiki provides no printer-board, USB, stepper, heater, thermistor, fan, endstop, or power connector pinout. The shared OctoPrint hostname is an access detail, not an electrical map.

    Visual evidence

    The page includes instance captions, but no readable wiring diagram in the inspected text. SoMakeIt printer-model wiki page.

    Evidence limits

    No firmware, mainboard revision, power supply, exact extruder revision, or present operational verification is stated. The old wiki source is an installation record, not a current manufacturer specification.

    Sources and revision limits

    The installation record and official versioned assembly references are separate evidence scopes. The source captures and exact original article were supplied in the frozen review packet; the official archive paths and three relevant assembly photographs were read live on 2026-09-27. No live SoMakeIt status is asserted.

    Wiki-recorded machine

    SoMakeIt identifies the SMI TAZ 5 as a LulzBot TAZ 3. The wiki lists a 280 × 280 × 250 mm print volume, PEI bed, 0.5 mm nozzle (explicitly marked for confirmation), and PLA/ABS. The unit has no OctoPrint address listed; file transfer is via SD card. Slicing software is listed as LulzBot Cura 21.08, Slic3r, or PrusaSlicer. The page labels status “functional,” also marked for confirmation.

    Use and limits

    Use the documented SD-card path and treat the nozzle size and status as unverified wiki entries requiring a local induction/check. The page does not give a model-specific start-up or maintenance sequence.

    Connections and visual

    No electrical, connector, control-board, thermistor, heater, stepper, or endstop pinout is published in the cited article. Its page contains an instance caption but no inspected wiring diagram. SoMakeIt printer-model wiki page.

    TAZ 3.0 manufacturer reference · not fitted-machine evidence

    The 2013Q4 LulzBot TAZ 3.0 User Manual identifies the Y-axis stepper/endstop connector pair, heated-bed heater/thermistor pair, and separate four-position hot-end and extruder-stepper plugs. Its setup photographs and text give the connector counts and group functions, but no per-cavity pinout. The manual shows a USB receptacle and keyed DC power receptacle without contact schedules. The official LulzBot engineering index lists TAZ 3.0 and 3.1 as distinct designs. An OHAI page under a taz_3 URL is explicitly titled “TAZ 2.1 Final Assembly” and was excluded as TAZ 3 evidence.

    LulzBot TAZ 6

    Research status: wiki-sourced model dossier; SoMakeIt records multiple differently configured instances. Captured 2026-09-23.

    Identity and instance distinction

    The SoMakeIt wiki lists SMI TAZ 01 as a LulzBot TAZ 6 and says TAZ 03 and TAZ 04 are also standard TAZ 6 units. TAZ 01 is listed functional, with a webcam, enclosure, 280 × 280 × 250 mm print volume, PEI surface, 1.2 mm nozzle, PLA/ABS/PETG, and Cura slicing with Cura, SD card, or OctoPrint transfer. TAZ 02 is described as a TAZ 6 with a 0.8 mm hardened-steel E3D hot end for flexible, abrasive, or high-temperature materials in addition to the TAZ 01 material list.

    The wiki has an unresolved naming conflict: it says “TAZ 3 and 4” are standard TAZ 6s, then labels “SMI TAZ 03” as “Prusa i3 MK3.” The two statements cannot safely be merged. This dossier attributes only the unambiguous TAZ 01/02 and the unambiguous TAZ 04 statement to the TAZ 6 model; TAZ 03 remains unresolved.

    Workflow and safety

    The page names Cura, SD-card transfer, and OctoPrint. It does not include a full print-start procedure. Follow the current machine-specific induction before use; this captured wiki page does not prove current status for every unit.

    Connections and pinout

    No electronics board, connector, heater, sensor, stepper, or power pinout is published on the cited wiki page. OctoPrint hostnames are not machine electrical interfaces.

    Visual evidence and source

    The page includes captions for the TAZ 01 and the TAZ 02 hot-end close-up, but no wiring diagram in the inspected text. SoMakeIt printer-model wiki page.

    Evidence limits

    This dossier records the wiki’s configuration differences and conflict; it does not assert that the printer fleet is currently active or that one instance’s settings fit another.

    Wiki sources

    The retained wiki dossier establishes local-machine identity. The separate manufacturer contact ledger above cites official wiring and assembly references; none proves the installed revision of SMI TAZ 01/02/04.

    OSE D3D Pro v20.07 3D printer

    Identity

    Open Source Ecology identifies D3D Pro v20.07 as the 8-inch-bed revision using the updated single-piece Universal Axis. It belongs to OSE's modular printer/fabrication family; this record is specific to the v20.07 design page.

    Wiki evidence

    • OSE D3D Pro v20.07: bed size, module architecture, scalability and development deliverable status.
    • OSE D3D: general modular printer and toolhead context.
    • OSE D3D Pro v20.07 development links: links to wiring/plumbing and build-instruction subpages.

    Architecture and operation

    The wiki describes five modules: gearless extruder, fast heated bed, Universal Axis motion system, multipurpose Universal Controller and Universal Frame. It says the 8 mm-axis version scales from an 18-inch bed design, with much larger scaling contemplated using a 1-inch axis. The page's development table marks design, electronics, wiring, BOM and build deliverables at 0%; this is an unfinished specification, not proof that the stated build is complete.

    Pinout and visuals

    No controller contact map is present in the captured page. Although a “Wiring and Plumbing” deliverable is linked, its existence in the table is not wiring evidence. Do not infer pins from the Universal Controller name.

    Status caveat

    Treat D3D Pro v20.07 as a documented design snapshot. Its listed “key specification” should not be treated as a validated performance result while the linked development checklist remains incomplete.

    Positron V.3

    Wiki-supported identity and facts

    The wiki catalogue lists a 180 × 185 × 180 mm build volume and describes an inverted print orientation and foldable portable form. Its linked wiki field is visibly a placeholder-domain URL, so no linked design documentation is treated as verified.

    Use, visuals, and electrical connections

    The captured wiki catalogue row does not provide a machine-specific operating procedure, connector table, electrical pinout, or transcribable wiring diagram. A separate creator-repository schematic documents six U7 support-PCB design contacts; those source-reference marks are reproduced individually below. They are not proof of this machine's installed board, a mating-face orientation, or a SmoothieBox route.

    Prusa CORE One 3D printer

    Identity

    RaumZeitLabor's current wiki homepage names “Prusa Core One” as a 3D printer and lists the hostname coreone for the lab's Prusa Core One printer. The spelling varies between “Core One” and “CoreOne.”

    Wiki evidence

    • RaumZeitLabor homepage: lists Prusa Core One among lab machines.
    • RaumZeitLabor network inventory: associates hostname coreone with a Prusa Core One 3D printer.

    Manufacturer electronics reference

    Prusa’s CORE One electronics guide applies to CORE One and CORE One+. It identifies the xBuddy main board and connected extension, a LoveBoard between xBuddy and Nextruder components, and a stepper splitter cable for the three Z motors. Its photos label several connector groups, but the guide provides no individual connector-contact schedule or signal-to-contact mapping. These describe the model family; the local wiki does not identify this lab printer’s exact board revision, fitted harness or mating views, so no generic electrical assignments are transferred. CORE One+ variants are excluded.

    Research limits

    The local wiki establishes identity and network naming only. The Prusa guide supplies board roles, not a revision-matched installed wiring map. No numbered contact schedule or electrical specifications suitable for SmoothieBox routing were recovered; connector counts and functions are not inferred from appearance.

    Pinout

    Unknown for the RaumZeitLabor unit. No contacts are individually assigned from the available sources, and every SmoothieBox-to-printer route remains OPEN.

    Sources and scope

    RaumZeitLabor establishes machine identity and hostname; Prusa provides a separate CORE One / CORE One+ electronics-family overview without a contact pinout.

    Prusa i3 MK3S+

    Research status: MakeICT wiki identifies its installed variant as MK3S+ under a shortened “Prusa i3 MK3” page title. Captured 2026-09-23.

    Identity and configuration

    MakeICT lists four Prusa3D i3 Mk3S+ units as operational. Its linked information page is titled “Prusa i3 MK3” and states the variant “Prusa i3 MK3s+.” It records 250 × 210 × 200 mm build volume, 1.75 mm filament, 0.4 mm nozzle, 300 °C maximum nozzle temperature, heated bed to 100 °C, automatic bed leveling, filament sensing, and head-crash detection.

    Wiki-recorded use

    The MakeICT page directs users to the FabLab’s general 3D-printing access policy/workflow. It says to clean the bed with isopropyl alcohol rather than acetone, check that the LCD’s selected bed matches the installed sheet, and avoid hairspray. For filament change, select a material preheat, unload, remove filament promptly, then insert the replacement and use auto-load/load if needed. The flexible steel sheet is removed by lifting its front corners and flexing it; the wiki says not to use scrapers.

    Connections and pinout

    The MakeICT pages provide model/inventory evidence, not an installed-board connector schedule. No inspected source establishes the controller model, controller revision, connector population or harness pinout of any individual MakeICT unit.

    Prusa's official MK3/MK3S/MK3S+ electronics-wiring article supplies EINSY RAMBo and 24 V model-family context. Its labelled overview identifies connector groups, not a numbered contact schedule for these local machines. It is not used to assign UltiMachine reference designators or pin numbers to MakeICT hardware.

    The added inventory is labelled Einsy Rambo 1.1a schematic reference only; installed controller/revision unknown. It transcribes the attached UltiMachine 11-sheet schematic dated 2017-09-18. It contains 24 connector references and 118 individually represented schematic terminals: 22 references / 106 terminals on sheets 2 and 5-11, plus X2 USB and X17 USB-side ICSP on sheet 4. The total includes P4 auxiliary terminals 9 and 10 and X2 shield terminals P$1 and P$2; it is not a count of cable cavities or installed accessible ports.

    J7 is the sheet-2 two-position 5V OUT reference (1 GND, 2 VCC). J16 is the sheet-5 two-position Power Fault Relay Connector 12-24V reference (1 GND, 2 toward nAC_FAULT through R69). X13 is one two-terminal heater connector drawn as X13A and X13B. J5 belongs to the FAN-0 circuit and J4 to FAN-1. J10 and J11 remain separate four-position Z-motor references. J15 numbers its temperature path as 1, Z_MIN path as 2, GND as 3 and VCC as 4; do not substitute a conventional probe-cable order.

    J19 is one 14-position header. Its positions 9-14 are also annotated ICSP for U2; they are not duplicated as a separate X18 connector. J19:8 is the R80/R81 divider junction, not the direct TX1 net. J19:13 is the R79/R82 junction feeding Q3 through R79, not the direct nRESET net. The ICSP annotation does not establish compatibility with a conventional programmer pinout or reset polarity. P2:10 reaches the U9 buffer input through FB32 and is not the direct MISO net.

    P4 is labelled RJ45 SMT, with eight interface positions and two additional symbol terminals connected to GND. Its positions 6 and 7 have no drawn wire or net label; their functions remain unknown rather than being assigned from a connector convention. Its R85/R86/R87 values are R0603TBD. P4 population, mating geometry and intended external use are not established; no Ethernet port is claimed.

    Contact labels preserve literal source nets. Where a connector-side node is unnamed, the inventory identifies only the drawn component path to a source label or device pin; that description is not a direct-net alias. Heater and fan switched terminals are not relabelled as their logic-control nets or as GND. Motor OA/OB references are not STEP/DIR inputs or fixed positive/negative motor leads. Literal +12V2 and +12V3 labels are retained without asserting installed voltage. USBVCC, GND1 and USHIELD remain distinct source labels.

    Every listed terminal has atlas route status OPEN, including source-labelled power and ground terminals. OPEN means no qualified external mapping; it does not mean the schematic terminal is electrically unconnected. There are no proposed electrical routes, relation edges, GUESS connections or DB25 peripheral. These are source-only machine-side reference cards opposite the unchanged SmoothieBox exterior.

X2 P$1/P$2 and P4 positions 9/10 are auxiliary shield/symbol terminals, not verified cable cavities. J19 pins 9–14 are counted once.     Connector numbering follows the named 1.1a schematic symbol, not a mating-face view. J1 uses printed pin numbers 1–6. X13A/X13B are units of one two-terminal X13 connector. The X2 P$1/P$2 shields and P4 9/10 terminals are retained as source symbols, not asserted as plug cavities. J13/J14 pin 1 is GND and pin 2 is X_MIN/Y_MIN through R74/R75. J15:1 is the Z_THERM path, J15:2 Z_MIN, J15:3 GND and J15:4 VCC. J19 pins 9–14 also carry the ICSP annotation and remain a single header. J10 and J11 remain distinct Z-motor outputs. Motor contacts are driver winding outputs, not STEP/DIR inputs.

    Visual evidence and source

    Reviewed 2026-09-28. MakeICT's model page and FabLab equipment inventory support the MK3S+ identity lead and the inventory's four operational entries. The model page's stock image does not establish the electronics revision of any installed unit.

    Prusa's official MK3/MK3S/MK3S+ wiring guide and its connector-labelled overview provide separate model-family context. The image includes a patch-board note restricted to version 1.0a and an MMU-related conditional label; neither proves a corresponding revision or accessory on MakeICT's machines.

    UltiMachine's Einsy Rambo 1.1a schematic is the sole contact-number and circuit-reference source for this added inventory. The reviewed attachment contains 11 pages; its locally verified SHA-256 is 6f0449efa84d8e90cafd963df8a4809ebd3c9d7fe760d1e3a8fe566a118aad3e. Sheet 1 identifies the revision/date; sheets 2, 4 and 5-11 establish the included connectors. The attachment, not a successfully re-fetched online PDF, is the reviewed byte source.

    Evidence limits

    Model naming follows MakeICT's body/inventory MK3S+ label while preserving its shorter page title. MakeICT inventory, Prusa model-family documentation and UltiMachine revision-specific design evidence are not interchangeable. No local unit is asserted to contain EINSY RAMBo, revision 1.1a, or every connector shown in this design.

    The sheet-1 entries about adding J7 as a power-failure input, moving RX1/TX1, combining ICSP, and changing the endstops belong to the historical 0.4a summary, not the 1.1a change list. The 0.5a summary records a further J19 pinout change. The actual 1.1a sheets control this transcription: J7 is 5V OUT and J16 is the power-fault connector. Do not infer that J16 is an X_MAX connector from its historical reuse.

    All contacts, including expansion/programming positions, J7, the X/Y endstop references, THERM2, Z_PROBE position 1 and P4, are schematic-only in this profile. Optional status, fitted population, current use and accessibility are unknown unless established separately. An unverified candidate is not labelled DNI or fitted merely because it appears in the schematic. P4:6 and P4:7 retain unknown functions; the mechanical role of P4:9 and P4:10 is not established by the schematic alone.

    No mating-face orientation, cavity drawing, wire colours, installed signal levels, load/current limits, external-device compatibility, firmware assignment or SmoothieBox mapping is established. Excluded from the connector count are mounting holes H1-H4, test points, fuses, reset switch S1, solder jumpers JP1/JP3/JP4, net ties and component pins. X13A/X13B are counted once as X13; J19's ICSP subset is counted once within J19. This is a source-reference inventory, not a wiring-ready qualification. Earlier diagrams remain retained and collapsed.

    Sources and scope

    Local wiki pages identify the machine only. Prusa’s guide supplies model-family board context; UltiMachine’s separate revision 1.1a schematic supplies revision-only contact references.

    Complete wiki-researched machine dossier

    Prusa i3 MK4

    Research status: MakeICT wiki lists an operational machine, but its wiki page says its usage information is “coming soon.” Captured 2026-09-23.

    Wiki-recorded configuration

    The MakeICT FabLab inventory lists a Prusa3D i3 MK4 as operational. Its model page records a 250 × 210 × 220 mm build volume, 1.75 mm filament, 0.4 mm nozzle, maximum nozzle temperature 300 °C, and maximum bed temperature 110 °C. The page uses a stock Prusa i3 MK4 image.

    Use information

    No model-specific print workflow was present in the inspected page; it explicitly says the printer information is still forthcoming. The inventory says the FabLab uses peer authorization for filament printers. No further use guidance is copied from non-wiki sources.

    Connections and pinout

    MakeICT controller revision and fitted accessories are unknown; Prusa publishes MK4 accessory-header references on the wiki page.

    Visual evidence and source

    The page includes a stock image, which does not prove the exact installed machine or revision. MakeICT Prusa i3 MK4 wiki page · FabLab inventory.

    Evidence limits

    The page was last revised in 2024 and contains no startup workflow, controller revision, machine photo, or revision-specific electrical evidence.

    Wiki sources

    Sources are restricted to the supplied wiki-research dossier. External vendor/forum links are not used as evidence.

    The supplied four-PDF inventory contains 48 connector/attachment groups and 329 individual source marks: 20 MP marks and four other shell/shield marks are recorded separately. Forty-two entries belong to DNF symbols and 25 have explicit source NC crosses; these categories overlap. All 329 routes are OPEN, and no dotted guess routes are proposed. All 82 SmoothieBox exterior contacts remain visible.

    Manufacturer revision references do not prove local fit. xLCD is a cross-model archive reference containing logical sheet 1/2 only; sheet 2/2 is absent. J21 pin 2 is printed SWDIO but has a drawn GND branch in xBuddy Rev 44; this source conflict remains unresolved. USB-C combined source marks are expanded individually and Ethernet PCB pads and mating jack contacts keep separate numbering domains. Numbered mounting points and shield marks are not signal harness pins. MP is not universally ground: LoveBoard fan MPs are HEATER_24V and thermistor-harness MPs are +24V.

    LoveBoard J14 traces are AVDD via L4, INNA via R3/L6 to HX-717 U2 pin 7, GNDA via L3, INPA via R4/L5 to U2 pin 8, plus a distinct GNDA MP. The Pressure_S graphic does not establish a net or force sign. LoveBoard J4 has no source-labelled axis. xBuddy J29 pin 2 is SCL, J15 is a temperature reference without an A_TEMP source label, and J6 TX-1/RX-1 paths retain their DNF E-STEP/E-DIR branches. Physical bridge orientation, firmware sign and all local cable continuity remain unknown.

    Prusa MK4S — FabLab Region Nürnberg

    Research capture: 2026-09-23. The FabLab Region Nürnberg wiki lists three Prusa MK4S printers as part of its FDM service. This dossier records the local inventory statement only; it does not claim three unique models or count the MK4S as a new product family relative to the separate MK4 dossier.

    Wiki-recorded operation

    The local 3D-printing page says these printers use 1.75 mm filament and a 0.4 mm nozzle as the FabLab's general FDM setup. Its general guidance requests STEP, STL, or 3MF input and lists FreeCAD, Blender, and OpenSCAD among software used. PLA and PETG are stocked; ABS, TPU, and ASA are not stocked and must be brought by the user. It requires a print form when starting a job and says charges depend on filament consumed, including failed prints. Time limits differ by event: KidsLab jobs are limited to 15 minutes or must start after 17:45; OpenLab jobs are limited to two hours or must start at the end of OpenLab.

    The wiki lists three Prusa MK4S units, each with a 250 × 210 × 220 mm build volume. It gives no unit identifiers, firmware versions, machine photos, controller/connector information, maintenance history, or machine-specific startup steps. The 1.75 mm filament and 0.4 mm nozzle values are stated in the shared FabLab printing section rather than a dedicated MK4S spec sheet.

    Pinout and visuals

    No electrical pinout or wiring diagram was found in the inspected wiki page. The page embeds a general 3D-printing video, which is not evidence of the three local printers' exact hardware. No local machine photograph or diagram is transcribed here.

    Source and identity limits

    Source: FabLab Region Nürnberg 3D printers wiki page. This is one local inventory/configuration record for three same-model units. A separate MakeICT dossier covers the MK4 generation; the Nürnberg MK4S is a distinct model revision but is conservatively treated as a family overlap for strict novel-machine counting.

    Complete supplied-source manufacturer review (2026-09-28)

    The shared archive drawings supply xBuddy Rev 44 (27 groups / 181 marks), LoveBoard Rev 38 (10 / 55), heatbed Rev 15 (2 / 2), and cross-model xLCD Rev 29 logical sheet 1/2 (9 / 91). Every mark is recorded in the current register and SVG, including MP, shell, source NC and DNF distinctions. All routes remain OPEN. The missing xLCD sheet and xBuddy J21 pin-2 source conflict remain explicit. This manufacturer schedule does not change the wiki’s local inventory evidence or establish fitted boards and cables.

    Sources and scope

    The FabLab wiki supplies local identity and operating evidence. The official Prusa archive supplies revision-scoped manufacturer contacts; installed local hardware and wiring are unverified. The MK4-only accessory article is excluded from MK4S assignments.

    Original Prusa XL — Bristol Hackspace configuration

    Wiki evidence status: exact printer model and five-tool local profile documented. The page does not identify the installed unit's serial number or firmware revision.

    Identity and configuration

    The Bristol Hackspace wiki describes a CoreXY Original Prusa XL with five tool positions and a 360 × 360 × 360 mm build volume. The documented local profile is “Prusa XL Original Prusa XL - 5T Input Shaper 0.4mm Nozzle.” It says the installation uses four high-flow ObXidian nozzles on tools 1–4 and a standard-flow ObXidian nozzle on tool 5. The machine uses 1.75 mm filament and a segmented bed with 16 independently controlled segments.

    Use notes

    The local wiki instructs users to slice with PrusaSlicer and use G-code or BG-code. For USB media it specifies FAT32 with an MBR partition table. It describes the five filament paths and recommends assigning the first colour and supports in the indicated tool lines, checking that slicer assignments match loaded material. The page cautions against ABS, ASA, HIPS, and PA unless an enclosure and advanced filtration system are in place; the bench-top filtration is stated to be insufficient.

    The page also records load/unload guidance, three available sheet types (smooth PEI, textured, and satin), and warns that inter-tool offsets can drift. It points users to the printer's tool-offset calibration wizard when this occurs. Induction is required.

    Pinouts and visual evidence

    The wiki describes a 32-bit custom control board, an expansion slot, and single-cable toolhead communication, but gives no board identity, connector pin map, or expansion-slot assignment. These architectural descriptions are not enough to identify electrical contacts. No wiring or pinout is inferred.

    The Bristol-hosted English XL handbook revision 1.04 (80 pages; PDF metadata modified 2024-06-11) says the mainboard has two extruder ports but gives no connector designators, contact counts, or contact assignments. Its tool-head overview names a toolchanger connector without listing contacts. The local wiki describes built-in Ethernet and Wi-Fi, a USB port, and one-cable tool-head communication; it contains no pin tables for those interfaces.

    Prusa’s current open-source index marks XL electronics schematics and the Dwarf, XLBuddy, XL Enclosure, and Modular bed board drawings as pending. The diagram therefore shows one model-family OPEN reference card for the two mentioned extruder-port groups and zero fabricated contact rows. Bristol’s installed board revision and five-tool expansion topology are unknown. No SmoothieBox route or dotted guess is proposed.

    Sources

    • Prusa XL — local 5-tool profile, operating guidance, materials, safety, and stated machine features.
    • Equipment catalogue — corroborates the Prusa XL listing.
    • Bristol-hosted Prusa XL handbook, English revision 1.04 — names two mainboard extruder ports without contact assignments.
    • Prusa open-source electronics index — current XL schematic publication status.

    Unknowns: serial number, firmware and hardware revisions, exact five-tool hardware configuration beyond the wiki note, control-board part number, and all electrical connector pinouts.

    Wiki sources

    Sources are restricted to the supplied wiki-research dossier. External vendor/forum links are not used as evidence.

    RepRap 1.0 Darwin

    Identity

    Darwin is the first RepRap rapid-prototyping machine design. It is an open, self-replicating FFF printer design, not a commercial product model.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRap Darwin: design history and legacy status.
    • RepRap 1.0 Darwin build overview: mechanism and nominal specifications.
    • RepRap-hosted Darwin figure: axis-labelled Cartesian overview; the wiki-hosted figure shows the XY carriage, Z bed, axes and nominal frame dimensions.

    Machine and operation

    The wiki describes an XY moving deposition head and a Z-moving bed, driven by steppers. Two fixed extruders are described for build and support material. Nominal working volume is 230 × 230 × 100 mm; the design is adjustable. The build instructions are linked from the wiki. The source gives USB computer interfacing and 12 V DC power, but not a universal controller board.

    Pinout and diagram transcription

    No universal Darwin connector schedule is established because the wiki describes a design family without binding a particular build to one electronics revision. The pinned RepRap Stepper Motor Controller Card v1.2 page, revision 151930, documents the P9 four-way 2.54 mm-pitch motor socket and source-numbered contact order. The table above transcribes all twelve X/Y/Z socket positions. X order is reversed relative to Y/Z in the source. These are motor winding outputs, not motion-controller STEP/DIR/ENABLE inputs. The card page separately lists PIC package pins; those are not connector contacts and are excluded. The machine figure labels axes and mechanism only; it does not map them to electrical contacts.

    Limits

    Darwin is retained for historical reference. Build volume, electronics and wiring vary by build.

    Wiki sources

    Sources are restricted to the supplied wiki-research dossier. External vendor/forum links are not used as evidence.
