    RepRap Wallace

    Identity

    Wallace is a parametric open-source Cartesian printer design described by the RepRap wiki as a robust redesign based on the Printrbot concept. Do not conflate it with Wally.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRap Wallace: design description, mechanism, dimensions and build-guide link.
    • Wallace build manual: assembly sections and example rod dimensions.
    • RepRap printer-by-picture index: visual catalog entry and comparison table.

    Specifications and operation

    The wiki says the design uses 6 mm smooth/threaded rods and NEMA 14 motors by default, with parametric alternatives. It reports a possible 200 × 200 × 140 mm build volume, 26 printed parts and approximately 0.07 mm X/Y and 0.025 mm Z positioning increments under the described microstepping. The manual covers X, Y, Z and bed assembly. The page is marked experimental/work-in-progress.

    Pinout and visuals

    The pinned Wallace design page labels electronics as a tentative parts-list category, and the mechanical build manual ends by directing the builder to wire electronics separately. Neither source names an installed or required controller revision or assigns motor, endstop, power, heater, thermistor or signal connector contacts. The printer-by-picture page is a comparison index, not a wiring schedule. No machine contacts or SmoothieBox routes are inferred.

    RepRap sources describe an experimental mechanical design and do not provide its electronics map.

    RepRapPro Huxley

    Identity

    RepRapPro Huxley is the RepRapPro-specific Huxley implementation. Its wiki explicitly supplies a complete build, wiring, commissioning, printing and maintenance guide set. Do not merge its wiring with other Huxley builds.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRapPro Huxley: model-specific frame/axis assembly and wiring navigation.
    • RepRapPro Huxley printing: slicer workflow, print-start sequence, filament change and operation.

    Operation

    The wiki recommends starting with the machine's tuned PLA/ABS profiles. It describes preparing STL to G-code in Slic3r/Pronterface, copying G-code to microSD, selecting SD Print, homing X/Y/Z, heating the nozzle and laying down an outline before the part. It cautions that USB printing can be interrupted by host scheduling or electrical noise.

    Wiring and diagram status

    The build guide has a dedicated wiring section and uses Melzi electronics in the pictured example. The full 41-position source inventory is transcribed in the interface register above; printed cavity numbering is retained only where the guide supplies it. The source's wiring diagrams should be interpreted only for the pictured RepRapPro/Melzi revision.

    Safety and limits

    The wiki instructs builders to read the complete build instructions before assembly. Temperatures and wiring must be matched to the installed hotend, bed and Melzi revision.

    Wiki sources

    The RepRapPro manufacturer wiring guide is scoped to its pictured Melzi build; the model-specific wiki pages do not establish local fitment.

    Smartrap Mini

    Identity

    Smartrap Mini is a GPL RepRap design inspired by Wallace. The wiki calls it a small, strong design intended to be simple to build and maintain; it contains numerous historical prototypes and revisions.

    Wiki evidence

    • RepRap Smartrap Mini: design intent, dimensions, materials, parts, prototype gallery and guide navigation.
    • RepRap machine index: model listing.

    Specifications and operation

    The wiki lists prototype print sizes between 150 × 150 × 150 and about 250 × 250 × 200 mm, with an early build at 200 × 200 × 150 mm. It describes PLA-only use as the design author's environmental choice, four NEMA 17 motors and three mechanical endstops. The wiki includes assembly and usage guides but notes that the assembly process remained under refinement.

    Pinout and visuals

    No controller model or pinout is specified. The page has a gallery labelled by prototype/version; match images and instructions to a revision before reuse.

    Limits

    The wiki marks the page's final update around the v0.4.5 development period and explicitly describes incomplete assembly documentation. Do not assume every gallery image depicts the same build.

    Source audit · 2026-09-28

    The pinned Mini revision lists four NEMA17 motors, one J-head hot end, one unidentified controller and three mechanical end stops. The separate V0.4.9 / 0.4.9.2 manual does not establish Mini electronics. No electrical contact positions, routes or DB25 are supported. The retained 227-position schedule is historical atlas material, not a Mini contact inventory.

    Four motor assemblies have no axis or winding map; the J-head has no heater/sensor pin schedule; the controller model is unknown; and the three end stops have no axis, terminal or NO/NC map. No dotted functional route is justified by the available sources.

    Acer Dynamic 1340G manual lathe — Artisans Asylum

    Wiki evidence status: exact model-specific local wiki page. The page identifies the serial as unknown and has a local user-manual attachment. This is a manual lathe, not a CNC machine.

    Identity and materials

    Artisans Asylum identifies the installed machine as an Acer Dynamic 1340G manual lathe. Its wiki page lists mild, alloy, and stainless steel; aluminum, brass, copper alloys, titanium; and PMMA/polypropylene as allowed material classes. It excludes wood, graphite, fibre composites, abrasive additives, and flammable or toxic materials.

    Operating and maintenance information

    The inspected wiki page refers users to a locally hosted Acer 1340G manual, a manufacturer manual, and a local copy. It gives lubrication guidance rather than a step-by-step turning procedure. For the apron gearbox, it lists Shell Tonna 33 and several ISO 68 slideway-oil equivalents. For the gearbox and headstock it lists Shell Tellus #27 / renamed Tellus 37, with Tellus S2 MX 32 or MX 46 among the named equivalents. Other oil points are to receive light machining or way oil. The page says to check the oil levels in the sight windows before each use or daily.

    Safety, visuals, and pinouts

    The wiki links to its metal-lathe safety notes. The article has no electrical pin map or CNC control information.

    The linked six-page owner manual, ACER 1340G User-man-v4.pdf, was inspected. Page 2 names the front-panel coolant-pump switch, jog button, power/emergency-stop button and speed/feed/threading controls. Page 4 labels the apron power-feed, threading and spindle forward/off/reverse lever; page 5 describes the foot pedal as a power-off/brake. These are operator controls and functions, not a numbered electrical connector map. The PDF supplies no machine-side cavity numbers, exposed control terminals, conductor assignments or electrical ratings, so none are drawn as SmoothieBox wiring points.

    Acer's Dynamic-1340G/1440E user-manual listing and circuit-diagram listing identify manufacturer support pages for this model family. The latter currently reports its linked PDF missing. The manual-lathe identity is not evidence of a CNC retrofit, an installed electronic spindle interface, or contact-level machine wiring.

    Sources

    • Acer Dynamic 1340G Manual Lathe — Artisans Asylum Wiki — model, material restrictions, manual links, and lubrication/checking notes.
    • ACER 1340G User-man-v4.pdf — Artisans Asylum Wiki attachment — six-page owner guide for operator controls and operating steps; no electrical connector map.

    Harrison M300 Lathe

    Research status: wiki-sourced model dossier. Captured 2026-09-23.

    Identity and training

    SoMakeIt identifies an owned Harrison M300 metalworking lathe. The wiki requires induction and says less-experienced operators are supervised until they have sufficient experience for unsupervised use. The source page does not provide a pinout or CNC retrofit evidence; this is a manual lathe.

    Workholding and tooling

    The wiki describes a self-centring three-jaw chuck for cylindrical/hex stock; a larger independent four-jaw chuck, adjusted with a dial indicator for concentric work; turning between centres using 60-degree centre holes; and a faceplate as a last-choice setup. It records a Dickson-style quick-change tool post. It distinguishes carbide inserts, high-speed steel, and brazed carbide, with material-dependent considerations; these are the space’s practical notes, not universal cutting parameters.

    Maintenance notes

    The wiki says to oil the machine’s oiling points daily, clean swarf/coolant and return tooling after use, check tailstock alignment and oil levels during inspection, and use ISO 68 slideway oil in specified locations. It directs users to check the gearbox-oil viscosity in the machine manual rather than supplying a value.

    Connections and pinout

    No electrical/control connector map or spindle-motor wiring is published on the cited wiki page. Do not infer the machine’s power arrangement from its product name.

    Visual evidence and source

    The page is tagged as missing its tool image; the inspected wiki text contains no wiring diagram. SoMakeIt Harrison M300 wiki page.

    Evidence limits

    The wiki is an operational community guide, not a manufacturer manual. Electrical ratings, exact installed options, serial number, and current status are not stated.

    Wiki sources

    Sources are restricted to the supplied wiki-research dossier. External vendor/forum links are not used as evidence.

    Schaublin 102-VM

    Research capture: 2026-09-23. Status: wiki-grounded draft; integration and whole-repository deduplication pending.

    Identity, use and deduplication

    FabLab Winti manual lathe. The machine directory labels the linked Drehbank page “Schaublin 102-VM”; the image also shows the model on the bed. This is distinct from the atlas Tormach/Sherline/Taig lathes. It is manual maker machinery, not a newly identified CNC retrofit.

    Wiki-supported machine facts

    Wiki specifies 16 × 16 mm tools and requires mechanical training and induction. It reports a tailstock center-height alignment problem at this installation; that is a local maintenance condition, not a universal 102-VM characteristic. Community machine page.

CNC homing, G-code and motion-controller setup are not applicable to the documented manual configuration. Motor starter ratings and terminals remain unknown. Community machine page.

    Charmhigh CHM-T36VA pick-and-place machine

    Evidence status: London Hackspace lists the exact model as working and training-required in a 2022 entry. Separate CHMT36VA community sources describe an STM32F407 controller, rear nine-pin RS-232 and USB-B camera-capture connections, and the machine subsystems below; installed revision and firmware are unverified.

    Identity and status

    London Hackspace lists “Charmhigh CHM-T36VA Pick-and-Place Machine” in its Fabrication inventory. The inventory says it is located in the Murder Kitchen, working, and training-required. The wiki entry was last updated 12 May 2022; that date means the status is historical and should not be treated as a live machine check.

    Model-specific interface evidence

    OpenPnP community material describes X/Y closed-loop steppers and encoders, Z lift, two nozzle-rotation steppers, feeder axes, X/Y home switches, a Z optical sensor, vacuum/blower/drag-pin actuators, cameras, lights and a buzzer. It identifies a rear nine-pin RS-232 connector and a USB-B port routed to the camera capture card. Charmhigh’s CHM-T36VA User Manual separately calls for a computer-side USB-to-serial cable and a USB camera cable, but gives no contact schedule. A separate community firmware repository maps logical STM32F407 GPIOs to functions but says official schematics are unavailable; those MCU assignments are not external harness contacts. The SVG lists DE-9 positions 1–9 as function OPEN and USB-B standard contacts 1–4; neither has a SmoothieBox route.

    Operation and wiring limits

    No verified external driver, sensor, actuator, or serial connector pin assignment is available for this installed unit. No polarity, electrical ratings, returns, mating view, or safety wiring is inferred. A direct SmoothieBox connection is not established.

    2026-09-26 original-project source update

    The project electronics drawing and Electronics Diagram table identify 23 peripheral cards without contact positions. The project-hosted SKR 1.4 Turbo pin map adds seven former-board connector cards and 27 OPEN printed marks: X, Y, Z Y-side, Z E0-side, E0 and E1 motor outputs each show 2B/2A/1A/1B; Z-STOP shows 5V/GND/1.27. The Z labels locate two board sockets, not two established machine Z axes or proof both are occupied. Motor-output marks are post-driver winding outputs, not SmoothieBox STEP/DIR inputs. None of these 30 cards proves a fitted PixiePlacer harness cavity or direct conductor. The table repeats 2.05 for Down LED and vacuum pump; project OpenPnP settings use a pump command there but do not resolve the physical LED or wiring. No SmoothieBox wire or dotted function guess follows.

    Smoothieboard/OpenPnP dual-head pick-and-place prototype

    Evidence depth: exact-project identity and selected build components are supported by the Appropedia catalogue and John Deglavina’s Hackaday project log. The separate OpenPnP-OpenBuilds source is an ancestor design, not proof of this prototype’s installed wiring.

    Direct-prototype sources and facts

    The Appropedia row names John Deglavina, calls this a working Smoothieboard/OpenPnP dual-head pick-and-place prototype, and says it is built on the OpenPnP-OpenBuilds model. The exact-project Hackaday log says it draws ideas from multiple machines and used OpenPnP-OpenBuilds as a starting point. It names a Smoothieboard 5X (initially acquired as 4X, then upgraded with added components), OpenBuilds frame parts, automatic feeders, and a RobotDigg dual head with linear rails. The log does not publish the installed connector cavity schedule.

    Electrical connections and source boundary

    The exact-project logs mention cameras, feeders, solenoids, a vacuum pump, and other build details, but do not establish their fitted connector cavities or Smoothieboard contacts. The OpenPnP-OpenBuilds instructions/configuration and diagram document a separate community build and its MCU software assignments; these are not the prototype’s physical contacts. Keep all such routes OPEN until an exact-project connector/harness source identifies both endpoints. No DB25 is evidenced.

    0816 source-model cable reference

    The exact-project BOM names the 0816 feeder. Its feeder-PCB v3 documentation lists +5 V, GND, servo PWM and feedback, and records feedback as added in v2. The source design uses one PCB per feeder. These four functions describe one reference cable, with fitted revision, feeder count, contact order, mating view, electrical contract and host pins unknown. The native Arduino Mega shield is a separate controller reference. No fan-out, shared return or SmoothieBox route is inferred.

    Epilog Zing 4030 laser cutter — FabLab Region Nürnberg

    Wiki evidence status: dedicated local machine page; marked functional in the wiki when inspected. The source describes a 30 W infrared laser with 406 × 305 mm working area (also given as nominal 400 × 300 mm in the local software setup).

    Local workflow

    The wiki uses VisiCut and Inkscape with SVG input; it also describes PDF input through Acrobat Reader. In the current VisiCut color convention, red is cutting, green is marking, blue is ignored, and black/other colors are engraving. SVG colors must be fully saturated, and Illustrator exports must use inline styling for VisiCut to read colors. For manually configured VisiCut settings, the wiki gives host zing1.fablab.lan, port 515, and a 400 × 300 mm bed size.

    The machine page documents locally tested material settings by material, power, speed, and frequency, and warns that those settings depend on clean optics. The wiki calls for weekly lens/mirror cleaning and monthly checks of light barriers and rails. It prohibits materials including PVC, PTFE/fluoropolymers, polyurethane, and ABS, and explicitly distinguishes true acrylic from craft “glass”. The wiki warns that operators must remain at the machine while it runs, with extraction and compressor running and a fire extinguisher nearby.

    Visuals and pinouts

    The page lists a machine photo, but it does not provide an electrical diagram or connector-level wiring map. Epilog's Zing-family service guide identifies an X-axis motor plug and a ribbon-cable connection on the X/Y Limit PCB; it does not publish contact counts, pin numbers, conductor functions, or mating views. The local unit's controller/PCB revision is unknown, so these named groups have unknown contact positions and no SmoothieBox routes. They are not a complete harness census.

    The local VisiCut host and port describe a software print-submission endpoint; they do not identify the machine's physical network connector or its pins. No pinout is inferred.

    Sources

    • ZING 4030 — FabLab Region Nürnberg Wiki — identity, local VisiCut configuration, material-specific settings, material restrictions, and operating workflow.
    • Lasercutter category — FabLab Region Nürnberg Wiki — confirms the Zing 4030 and Nova 35 are distinct local lasers.
    • How to Replace the Home Switch (XY PCB) — Epilog Zing Support Center — family-level evidence for the named X-axis motor and X/Y Limit PCB ribbon interfaces; no pin schedule.

    Unknowns: serial number, tube/optics revision, current calibration, exact settings database revision, fitted controller/PCB revision, physical network connector, electrical schematics, contact counts, cavity identities, conductor functions, and connector pinouts.

    3D FabLight 3000 W sheet-metal laser

    Identity

    Artisans Asylum's wiki identifies a 3D FabLight sheet-metal laser, model recorded as “3,000 Watt,” serial 30450. That model field is a power designation in the wiki, not a conventional alphanumeric model number.

    Wiki evidence

    • Artisans Asylum 3DFabLight page: machine identity, supported sheet materials/thicknesses, operation prerequisites and startup sequence.
    • The page says the machine cuts thin sheet metal using a laser and air pressure. It requires both AC plugs, shop air, extraction, a closed door, released E-stop and homing before jobs.
    • Its material restrictions explicitly exclude stainless steel, galvanized/painted/coated stock and all non-metals, with fume/fire warnings.

    Operation and visuals

    The wiki directs operators to its operation manual and FabCreator instructions. It describes the offline → initialized → machine-not-homed → homed state sequence. The wiki page includes machine/control imagery; it does not provide an electrical connector map in the reviewed text.

    Pinout

    The local wiki has no controller pinout. A 2021 FabLight 1500/3000/4500 operator manual names Utility Panel connections and documents the VACUUM/VACUUM POWER cord-end forms. The exact manual revision and its ports are not confirmed for serial 30450. Its two IEC reference groups show only the standard L, N and PE functions, without mating-face orientation; each remains OPEN to SmoothieBox.

    Family-level Utility Panel reference

    • Main Power input plug, Ethernet, VACUUM outlet and VACUUM POWER inlet are named on the manual’s Utility Panel; the local serial’s connector revision remains unverified.
    • GAS IN and GAS EXHAUST are distinct 3/8-inch tube interfaces. The manual warns that pressurised input belongs only at GAS IN.
    • The manual identifies a rear exhaust-duct port, plus an I/O panel with MAINS and ON indicators, a momentary key switch, and an Emergency Stop. These are not SmoothieBox pin assignments.
    • The manual’s cord descriptions imply a C13 appliance outlet at VACUUM and a C14 appliance inlet at VACUUM POWER. Their source-scoped terminal labels are L (line), N (neutral), and PE (protective earth); physical pin order and installed fit remain unverified.
    • Every family-reference position is OPEN. No mains, network, pneumatic, interlock, or control route to SmoothieBox is proposed; no dotted guesses are drawn.

    Scope

    This is industrial sheet-metal laser equipment and a distinct machine class from the CO₂ gantry cutters elsewhere in this research set.

    Sources

    1. Artisans Asylum 3DFabLight page — local machine identity, serial 30450, operator workflow, and limits of the local wiring evidence.
    2. FabLight Operator’s Manual v4.3 (2021), pp. 15–18 — manufacturer-authored 1500/3000/4500 family Utility Panel and control references; PDF metadata title says v4.2, while printed page footers say v4.3.
    3. Interpower IEC 60320 C13 connector drawing, form 83012521 — standard terminal roles L, N, and protective earth; not proof of the FabLight unit’s fitted connector revision.
    4. IEC 60320-1:2015 appliance-coupler standard — appliance inlet/outlet scope. No C13/C14 mating-face orientation is asserted here.

    Research status: wiki-sourced machine dossier; whole-repository deduplication is complete for the exact model string, while visual and electrical evidence remain incomplete. Captured 2026-09-23.

    Identity and status

    SoMakeIt’s wiki identifies its laser as manufacturer HPC, model “laserscript 1290,” and elsewhere calls it an “HPC 1290.” Keep both spellings as source labels; do not infer the separate “LS1290 PRO” suffix that appears only in an external datasheet link. The wiki says Southampton University donated the machine. It requires member training and must not be operated unattended.

    Wiki-recorded configuration and workflow

    • Cutting area: 1200 × 900 mm, slightly reduced for engraving.
    • CO₂ glass tube, water cooled by a compressor-based chiller; exhaust vents outside; air assist is present.
    • Wiki-listed engraving speed: up to 400 units/second; the page says faster settings reduce quality, but does not specify the meaning of the speed unit.
    • Z table travel/height: 230 mm.
    • Computer or USB connectivity; LightBurn is the named software.
    • A rotary attachment is recorded. The wiki describes aligning it on bed slots, connecting it to an internal port near the right-hand control panel, re-zeroing axes, setting the Y scale to 195%, enabling rotary mirroring and using 120 lines per inch. These are page-specific setup notes; the source says the “Send” path is recommended because “Start” had not been tested with the rotary.

    Before use, the wiki requires training, a fire plan, ready fire blanket/extinguisher, clear machine and area, exhaust operation, and use of materials cleared by the space. It says never leave the cutter unattended. It warns against PVC and polycarbonate; material clearance is required for anything not previously assessed.     2026-09-26 source update · original board versus Winti build

    The Lasersaur Driveboard v14.03 wiring page assigns functions on twelve eight-position RJ45 cables for limits, motor windings, doors, laser, chiller, E-stop and optional E-valve. The X/Y motor cables terminate after the original drive stage; original door, chiller and E-stop interlocks form a hardware safety chain. The Winti machine page confirms local modifications and a 100 W laser, cooling, ventilation and E-stop, but supplies no revision-matched installed cable continuity or laser PSU electrical contract.     HPC LaserScript LS6090 — CoMakingSpace configuration

    Wiki evidence status: named machine configuration with detailed local controls and material notes. The wiki says the supplier was HPC Lasers and rates the installed CO₂ system at 80 W; tube/controller revisions are not recorded.

    Identity and setup

    The CoMakingSpace wiki identifies this machine as a LaserScript LS6090 supplied by HPC Lasers. It lists 80 W power, a 600 × 900 mm worktable, and 230 mm Z height. The listed software is LaserCut 5.3, with a laser exhaust system and water chiller. The page's status note says the cutter was not usable until its fire extinguisher had been replaced; this historic wiki status needs current local confirmation before anyone treats the machine as usable.

    Controls and operation

    The wiki describes a right-side machine control panel. On startup, the operator presses “Datum” to home the head to the upper-right corner. With no menu item highlighted, direction keys jog the head. Jog travel is configured through Menu → Down → Down → Enter. The page describes focusing with a physical focus gauge on the material while raising the tray until the gauge just slides through. Uploaded jobs are started or paused with “Start / Pause.”

    The source identifies LaserCut 5.3 and points to a dedicated wiki material-settings page. It lists exhaust filtration and a water chiller as required associated equipment. The wiki does not supply controller firmware or machine-specific G-code.

    Pinouts and diagrams

    No electrical connector, laser power-supply terminal, controller-board identity, or pin assignment appears in the captured wiki evidence. The page shows illustrations of the control panel and a “CANCEL LOGIC ORG” recovery sequence, but these do not establish machine wiring. No electrical pinout has been inferred.

    Rabbit QX-80-1290 laser cutter

    Research status: wiki-sourced machine-specific dossier; the exact model string is absent from the existing repository search. Captured 2026-09-23.

    Identity and wiki-recorded configuration

    MakeICT’s FabLab list identifies an operational Rabbit Laser QX1290; its dedicated laser page names the machine Rabbit QX-80-1290. The two wiki forms are retained as aliases because the inventory omits the “80” portion. The page records a 1200 × 900 mm bed, 80 W sealed CO₂ tube, approximately 10-inch maximum bed height, 300 mm/s maximum cutting speed, 600 mm/s maximum engraving speed, and 1000 DPI maximum engraving resolution. LightBurn is the stated interface.

    Wiki-recorded operation

    The community guide requires authorization, never leaving the powered cutter unattended, not bypassing safety switches, and using only approved materials. Its summarized job sequence is:

    1. Prepare artwork and import it to LightBurn.
    2. Confirm design size, layer operation, order, speed and power; preview the tool path.
    3. Badge-authorize and power on the machine; confirm compressor, exhaust fans and chiller are on.
    4. Let homing finish; position and focus the material; use the frame function to check job bounds.
    5. Close the lid and start the job. Remain present; after completion the wiki recommends waiting about 30 seconds before opening to vent fumes.

    The wiki’s listed settings are starting points that vary with material and day. The cited article directs users to test small areas and to use its material approval list; no external material guide was used here.

    Thunder Laser Nova 35 — FabLab Region Nürnberg

    Wiki evidence status: dedicated local page; the wiki marks the Nürnberg installation functional. The page lists Thunderlaser/Allplast as maker, a Nova 35 model, a roughly 80 W laser, and a 900 × 600 mm work area. The wiki notes that the Nova 35 installations in Nürnberg and Veitsbronn have different tubes; this dossier is scoped to Nürnberg.

    Local setup and software

    This laser is available only after instruction and is not approved for open-lab use, according to the wiki. The local workflow recommends Inkscape with VisiCut; RDWorks is named as the Windows-only software supplied with the laser. VisiCut can connect over the local network at 172.22.30.50 / nova35.fablab.lan, or use USB storage or serial USB (/dev/ttyUSB0 on Linux, COM4 as one Windows example). The page warns that many VisiCut “recommended” material profiles are wrong or untested and asks users to use a small test cut and compare the material table.

    Preparation and operation

    Before use, the wiki instructs the operator to connect the Nova's exhaust hose to the external extraction, power the extraction, switch on the laser and press its red reset button. The machine needs the lid closed for the display/reset sequence. Material is placed on the bed and held with magnets or weights if needed. The operator uses the cursor keys and start-position control, then the Box function to preview the job bounds. For focusing, the page describes using the supplied 20 mm gauge between nozzle tip and material surface.

    After transferring the file, the local procedure checks the extraction setup, selects Auto and Nova on the extraction controls, then starts with Start/Pause and verifies that the ventilation runs. The wiki says to wait about 30 seconds after cutting for smoke to clear. It warns that the head can move quickly and the blue nozzle sits only 20 mm above the work, creating a collision risk.

    The local wiki includes a material table with power, speed, minimum power and frequency. These are installation-specific starting values; the page notes the other Nova 35 has a different tube and directs users to test settings.

    Visuals and pinouts

    The page lists machine photos but no readable wiring schematic or connector map. Network and USB connection details describe data transfer, not electrical pin assignments. No pinout is inferred.

    Sources

    • Nova 35 — FabLab Region Nürnberg Wiki — identity, status, local controls, setup, software, operating sequence, risks, and material table.
    • Lasercutter category — FabLab Region Nürnberg Wiki — distinct local inventory entry alongside the Zing 4030.

    Unknowns: exact tube and controller revision in Nürnberg, serial number, calibration status, wiring diagrams, connector assignments, and current approval/training state.

    Manufacturer family reference · contact inventory and limits

    The 2018 Nova 35 manual’s panel/machine-view figures (printed pp. 23, 29) show two USB Standard-A ports (PC and U-disk) and Ethernet. The USB positions follow USB-IF Standard-A contact functions; Ethernet positions 1–8 are counted by 8P8C form because the manual provides no signal mapping. The TL-Timer figure (printed p. 34) shows four three-position channel blocks (CH1 warning lamp, CH2 spare, CH3 exhaust fan, CH4 spare) and two positions each for interfaces 9 (lid state), 10 (working state), and 11 (5 V DC supply). The drawing labels interface 11 +5V/GND. Timer slot letters in the diagram are editorial counting marks, not manufacturer terminal numbers; other timer terminal functions and polarities are OPEN.

    Inventory: PC USB 1–4 (VBUS, D−, D+, GND); U-disk USB 1–4 (same USB Standard-A signal names); Ethernet positions 1–8 (function OPEN); CH1–CH4 positions A–C (function/polarity OPEN); interfaces 9 and 10 positions A–B (function/polarity OPEN); interface 11 positions A (+5V in the manual illustration) and B (GND in the manual illustration). All 34 remain unrouted. The USB/Ethernet ports are data connections; compatibility with SmoothieBox is not established.

    This is a family-manual reference, not verified Nürnberg fitment. The local wiki does not specify controller board or TL-Timer revision, and the 2018 manual is not evidence of installed revision. No mains, heater, laser, fan, or interlock wiring is proposed. The current Thunder Laser “NOVA Series Wiring Diagram TL Timer V8.4” article was checked; its linked assets did not yield a readable pin schematic. Sources: 2018 Nova 35 user's manual; USB-IF USB 2.0 Specification; Thunder Laser TL Timer V8.4 article.

    Thunder Laser Nova 63 — Dallas Makerspace

    Research capture: 2026-09-23. Dallas Makerspace's laser wiki names its large-format unit “Big Thunder,” a Thunder Nova 63.

    Wiki-recorded configuration and operation

    The wiki lists a 1600 × 1000 mm work area and 130 W output. Its general Thunder Nova notes state that Nova 35 and Nova 63 machines use servo systems described as steppers with optical encoders. The page warns that detected skipped steps can make a machine stop tracking its position and crash the head; it says Reset forces a re-home. It notes the same loss-of-position issue may occur with the rotary attachment. The community wiki requires its Laser Basics certification class for Thunder lasers and describes the curriculum as covering safety, RDWorks, and Thunder operation.

    The same page identifies two separate Nova 35 units, Donner and Blitzen. They are not counted as separate model identities in this dossier, and this Nova 63 dossier is kept distinct from the existing Nova 35 entry. The generic servo and reset guidance applies to both families per the wiki; the page does not establish Nova-63-specific controller parameters or wiring.

    Connections and visuals

    No controller board revision, motor connector, laser supply, limit input, or pin/contact assignment was found in the inspected wiki source. The page links to manufacturer manuals, but those external documents were not used. The category page lists the local unit and operating notes but does not provide an inspected machine-specific wiring illustration.

    Source and limits

    Source: Laser committee wiki page — Dallas Makerspace. This is a community equipment record, not a revision-specific wiring reference. It identifies the local model and some operating guidance; all unlisted electrical details remain unknown.

    Manufacturer Nova Series family-manual reference and contact limits

    The Thunder Laser Nova Series Unified User Manual covers Nova 24, 35, 51 and 63. Its machine-view text names PC USB, U-disk USB and Ethernet ports, and locates TL-Timer hardware inside the Nova 35/51/63 enclosure. It also names laser supply and chiller power sockets, exhaust and blow-air ports, Water IN/OUT, and a No-Water protection signal port. The Dallas page does not identify its installed controller, timer revision, chiller configuration, or connector pinouts.

    The manual's TL-Timer section (printed pp. 57–58) individually names OUT1–OUT8, 5V Output 1, 5V Output 2, Upgrade, 24V Input, and In1–In8. Their source-listed functions are shown in the linked detailed schedule. These are interface/function IDs, not physical terminal positions; the manual does not provide terminal cavity counts or individual pin signal/polarity assignments for these groups. All 20 references remain OPEN. Manual-designated spare interfaces are not relabeled as electrical NC.

    The 2024 unified manual is kept separate from older Nova-35 timer schedules. No mains, laser-power, heater, exhaust, air-assist or safety wiring is proposed. Sources: Thunder Laser Nova Series Unified User Manual; Nova Series Wiring Diagram TL Timer V8.4.

    Dake SB-32V drill press — Artisans Asylum

    Wiki evidence status: exact model and local operating instructions documented. The wiki lists two units, one in each of the Metal Shop and Machine Shop; serial numbers and unit-specific differences are not identified.

    Controls and operation

    The wiki describes the Dake SB-32V as reversible with variable speed. To start, release the emergency stop and use the three-position switch to select direction; the page says forward is appropriate for nearly all normal use. A small black knob adjusts spindle speed over a moderate range. To stop, set the switch to OFF or press the emergency stop.

    For larger speed changes, the wiki's sequence is to unplug the machine, open the belt/pulley cover, loosen the belt-tension lock, select the belt arrangement from the local table or the referenced page in the manual, move the motor to tension the belt, close the cover, then reconnect power. The page notes the belt should deflect about 1/2 in under finger pressure. It describes an idler pulley in the drive train.

    The general drill-press wiki category says to secure the workpiece, keep guards in place, wait for the tool to stop before unloading, and never side-mill with a drill press. The page identifies the shop units' restriction state as green; current local authorization rules remain authoritative.

    Visuals and pinouts

    The wiki page includes images labelled as the machine, speed control, and pulley set. These illustrate visible controls and belt arrangement; they do not reveal internal wiring or connector assignments. No pinout is present in the inspected wiki article.

    Do-All 2013-1 metal-cutting vertical bandsaw — Artisans Asylum

    Wiki evidence status: exact model and local configuration documented. The wiki dates the installed machine to 1977 and describes it as an antique. Its referenced instruction manual is for a similar model; a separate 2013-1 service manual is identified.

    Local configuration and operation

    Artisans Asylum identifies a Do-All 2013-1 vertical band saw in its Machine Shop. The wiki says its high-speed range is disabled, leaving only the low range available. The saw is usually set up for mild steel; the page directs users to determine an appropriate blade speed for other materials, then check the feet-per-minute indicator while the saw is running.

    Power controls are at the rear, and a work lamp is available. A crank near the lower left changes blade speed and, according to the wiki, must only be turned while the machine is running. A separate rear crank formerly selected low/high range and is clamped out of use. The saw has an integrated spot-welder for joining blade stock; instructions are printed on the welder's front panel.

    General metal-cutting vertical-band-saw guidance on the wiki calls for guards in place, the blade guard set close to the work, the work kept flat and secure, cutting oil, and waiting for the blade to stop before removing stock from a partial cut.

    Visuals and pinouts

    The article contains local photographs/captions for the rear power switch, speed indicator, speed crank, and blade welder. They document visible machine controls but no wiring or connector assignments. No electrical pinout is published on the inspected wiki pages.

    HydraFabber multi-tool CNC prototype

    Identity

    Open Source Ecology's wiki describes HydraFabber as a portable, multi-headed CNC fabrication-machine concept intended to combine 3D printing, circuit milling and laser cutting. The wiki says the build was preceded by HydraRaptor and was intended for OSE design sprints; it is a prototype/design, not an established commercial model.

    Wiki evidence

    • OSE HydraFabber: intended functions and high-level specifications.
    • OSE Personal Microfactory: identifies the related D3D platform and alternative fabrication toolheads.

    Functional information

    The wiki sets a minimum 200 × 200 × 120 mm print volume, quick-change heads with repeatable alignment, a suitcase-style travel case and a target setup time under ten minutes. It describes a 1.5 W diode laser and a circuit-mill head with depth control and quick-change PCB holding. A separate OSE microfactory page describes a 4 W diode for a related D3D platform; that different power figure is not silently applied to HydraFabber.

    Pinout and visuals

    No controller revision or connector pinout is specified on the HydraFabber page. Its wiki-embedded video and linked equipment page are design/process evidence only; no contact-level wiring diagram was recovered.

    Status and uncertainty

    The wiki page itself is an exploratory project record. Requirements do not prove all heads were built or validated. Treat it as a named prototype concept, not a production-ready machine.

    Nichols Model 10-B Therm-O-Vac

    Research status: wiki-sourced vacuum-former dossier; exact model absent from the existing repository search. Captured 2026-09-23.

    Identity and configuration

    The MakeICT FabLab inventory lists an operational Nichols model 10-B Therm-O-Vac from Industrial Arts Supply Co. Its machine page records a 14 × 20 inch frame, thermoplastic sheet thickness of approximately 0.5–1.5 mm, and a single three-way switch.

    Wiki-described process and use

    The wiki describes placing a mold over a perforated surface, clamping and heating plastic until it softens, then drawing it over the mold with vacuum. The resulting sheet follows the mold contour. The page gives approximate heating times by thickness: HIPS/PETG 15/30/45 seconds for 0.5/1/1.5 mm sheets; ABS 20/40/60 seconds. It warns that these values are approximate and says the machine cannot heat LDPE sufficiently for forming.

    The page says the access policy had not yet been established at its last edit. Do not assume the machine is currently available or that this page is a sufficient safety/operating induction.

    Connections and pinout

    Only a single three-way operator switch is identified. The wiki does not label switch positions, terminals, supply voltage, heater circuit, vacuum pump wiring, or protective devices. No numbered pinout or schematic is published.

    Visual evidence

    The article embeds an image identified as the Nichols Model 10-B, plus a wiki-linked video of that machine in use. The image remains at the wiki because the page’s image reuse license was not verified. MakeICT Vacuum Former wiki page · FabLab inventory.

    Evidence limits

    Frame size and process notes are community-wiki claims. Heater temperature, vacuum level, electrical ratings, and verified material compatibility are not specified.

    The wiki describes an oxy-fuel or plasma torch table for cutting large/detailed parts. These notes are revision-specific and should not be used to bypass a safety or temperature interlock on other hardware.

    Pinout and diagrams

    The wiki includes an electronic-system diagram link and CAD for the Smart Controller, SSR and TB6600. The captured page does not expose numbered board connector assignments. Transcribe those diagrams from the exact v19.10 files before connecting power, motor or gas-control signals.

    Variant warning

    The 2021 v21.08 machine and unbuilt v19.06 concept are separately named by the genealogy. Do not treat their wiring as identical to v19.10.

    Wiki evidence status: exact oven model with a local modification and operating page. The modification revision and current firmware version are not stated.

    Identity and configuration

    Bristol Hackspace identifies this as a T-962 solder reflow oven and gives an effective soldering area of 180 × 235 mm. Its local unit differs from an untouched factory configuration: the cardboard insulation was removed and replaced with aluminium tape, a cold-junction temperature sensor was added, and the firmware was flashed. The wiki links the firmware repository, but this dossier uses only the wiki's description and does not infer a board revision or firmware build.

    Operation

    The local instructions say to place the oven on a heat-proof mat, power it on, and put the PCB on the rack. Press F4 to open profile selection, use F1/F2 to select a profile, press S to choose it, then press S to start. Manual mode opens with F3; F1/F2 set temperature, F3/F4 set a timer, and the countdown begins after preheating. When the timer expires, the oven begins cooling.

    Electrical connections and diagrams

    The wiki page does not provide a connector pinout, wiring diagram, temperature-sensor terminal assignment, or a detailed controller-board identity. No wiring map is inferred from the T-962 model name. The page contains no machine-specific diagram transcription beyond the stated rack and interface-key procedure.

    Safety

    The wiki warns that the PCB and oven underside may remain hot after reflow, including during the cooling phase. Use heat-resistant placement and handle the board only after it has cooled.

    Sources

    • Solder Reflow Oven — T-962 — exact local machine identity, area, modifications, and controls.
    • Electronics Room inventory — corroborates the machine's listing in the room inventory.

    Unknowns: exact firmware source revision and build, sensor wiring, controller PCB revision, mains/thermal wiring, and any changes made after the wiki page's last revision.
